If you are a priest, bless and absolve me father. I hope this finds you well. Please don’t see below as an attack I just had a concern about something in the John’s Repentance group that I needed to address. 

I saw the answer to the makeup question in Johns repentance and was a bit confused. Everything I’ve learned from so far with teachings of the fathers and other writings have taught me that it is in fact something we are not supposed to take part in at all. I’m concerned by the answer because it allows for a small but possibly dangerous leeway for us as women and girls to think it’s ok when in fact it’s not and does no good for us whether in body or soul. Can you kindly please tell me which church fathers or which books you cite that agree with your stance that it’s ok as long as the intention is pure?

Here are some sources I’ve learned from that say otherwise.

“He commits a serious offense who adulterates the work of God. It is a serious charge to suppose that man is to be preferred to God as an artist! It is serious, indeed, when God has to say this about you: 'I do not recognize My colors or My image, not even the countenance which I have made. What is not Mine I reject. Take up your abode with him who has painted you. Seek your favors from him to whom you have given payment.' What will be your reply?” St Ambrose

Apostolic Constitutions book 1 par 8 (400 ad)
Do not paint thy face, which is God's workmanship; for there is no part of thee which wants ornament, inasmuch as all things which God has made are very good. But the lascivious additional adorning of what is already good is an affront to the bounty of the Creator.

Blessings and peace to you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,

Thank you for bringing your concerns forward with a spirit of inquiry and faithfulness. In the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, we hold dear the teachings of our Fathers and the sacred traditions that have been entrusted to us. Your question regarding makeup is an important one, as it relates to how we present ourselves before God and others.

As you rightly pointed out, our Church Fathers, including St. Ambrose and others, have spoken about the dangers of adorning oneself in ways that detract from the natural beauty that God has bestowed upon us. In the spirit of their teachings, the use of makeup should be approached with great caution and discernment.

The Apostolic Constitutions reminds us that our primary adornment should be the "hidden person of the heart," as noted in 1 Peter 3:3-4. The focus is on cultivating inner beauty — a beauty that reflects our devotion, humility, and love for God.

While the previous answer mentioned that makeup is not inherently sinful, it is crucial to emphasize that in our tradition, simplicity and naturalness in appearance are valued highly as expressions of humility and purity of heart. The use of makeup can easily lead to vanity and a focus on external appearances, which is contrary to the spirit of Orthodox Christian living.

Therefore, in alignment with the teachings of our Church Fathers, I would advise caution and restraint in the use of makeup, always examining one's intentions and seeking to glorify God in all things, including our appearance. However blindly labeling makeup as sin without analyzing the situation would not be fully aligned with the Church's definition of sin.  

In this regard, consider how you can cultivate the beauty of your soul through prayer, fasting, and acts of charity. How might your outward appearance reflect the inner transformation that is taking place in your heart as you draw nearer to God?

May the peace of Christ guide your heart and mind in all things. Amen.

text: Behoved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, let us delve into a comprehensive lesson about marriage. This exploration aims to imbue the reader with deep understanding and reverence for the sacred institution of marriage as seen through the Orthodox Christian perspective.

text.text: The Essence of Marriage: A Divine Union

text: Marriage, as understood in Orthodox Christianity, is not merely a social contract or a means to personal fulfillment. It is a holy sacrament, an eternal bond sanctified by God. In the Orthodox tradition, marriage symbolizes the mystical union between Christ and the Church, as articulated by St. Paul in his Epistle to the Ephesians (5:25-32). It is a path towards holiness, a journey that spouses embark upon together, aiding each other in their spiritual growth and salvation.

text.text: The Purpose of Marriage: Beyond the Mundane

text: Orthodox Christianity teaches that the purpose of marriage extends beyond companionship and procreation. While these are significant aspects, the true purpose lies in the spiritual edification of both partners. Marriage is a vocation to love as Christ loves, sacrificially and unconditionally. It's a call to nurture not only children but also the fruits of the Spirit within each other – love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23).

text.text: Choosing a Spouse: A Discerning Heart

text: In selecting a life partner, the Orthodox faith emphasizes the importance of spiritual compatibility. It's not merely about finding someone with shared interests or attractions but about finding a partner who shares a commitment to Christ and His Church. This spiritual congruence forms the bedrock of a marriage that can withstand the trials and tribulations of life.

Marriage, in its truest Orthodox essence, is not free from challenges. However, these trials are seen as opportunities for growth and deepening of faith. The Church teaches that through mutual sacrifice, forgiveness, and unconditional love, couples can mirror the love of Christ. In times of conflict, turning to prayer, the sacraments, and the guidance of spiritual fathers can be invaluable.

text.text: The Role of Community and Tradition

text: In Orthodox Christianity, marriage is not just a union of two individuals but a communal sacrament. The Church, the body of Christ, plays a vital role in supporting and nurturing marital relationships. The rich traditions and rituals of the Orthodox wedding ceremony, such as the crowning and the common cup, symbolize the deep spiritual truths of marriage – sovereignty in serving one another and sharing life’s joys and sorrows.

text.text: Eternal Perspective: Marriage as a Journey to the Kingdom

text:
Ultimately, Orthodox marriage is viewed in the light of eternity. It’s a journey towards the Kingdom of Heaven, where each spouse helps the other in their path to salvation. This eternal perspective infuses every aspect of married life with profound significance and purpose.

In conclusion, marriage in the Orthodox Christian sense is a sacred journey of love, sacrifice, and spiritual companionship. It's a covenant blessed by God, intended for the mutual salvation of the spouses and the glorification of His holy name. May this exploration of Orthodox marriage inspire and guide those seeking to understand and embody its true essence.

text.text: 👉🏾 Question from member: I often feel depressed and lonely. Life has no meaning to me, I just want to die and live with Jesus, I've been looking for happiness all my life but I can't find it, I feel like my mind is going to explode, please pray for me, I need prayer, what do you recommend?

text:
Why does a person choose loneliness? Why does a person hide? In essence, man is not happy without God, because there is no peace without God. Jesus Christ said in the Gospel of John, chapter 14, verse 27, "Peace I leave with you, and my peace I give you, the peace I give you is not as the world gives; do not let your hearts be troubled, do not be afraid."
 
The world kisses us today then bites tomorrow; gives today then takes away tomorrow. But God does not take away what He has given, no matter what, there is no peace without God. What is life? Life is the opposite of death, life is living. Life is God, it is written, "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life."
 
Therefore, if we believe in the Son, we live with Jesus who is the life. It is Jesus Christ who gave life when human beings could not live according to the commandment, it is Jesus Christ who enlightened the dark world. In fact, this Christmas (birth) season is called the light. And if it is said who is the light: it is Jesus Christ.

This world was dark before God the Son became a man. The world lived in darkness. It is called light because God became a man and enlightened the world by making us members of His body. Many people's lives are in darkness. Darkness is sin, darkness is betrayal, darkness is hatred, darkness is lack of love; On the other hand, light is Jesus Christ, light is life, light is religion, light is peace, light is help, blessing and love. Because it is our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ who gave us that, there is no life without Jesus Christ.
 
As the owner himself told us, John Gospel chapter 15 verse 5 said "without me you can do nothing", so without Jesus Christ nothing can be done. How can peace be found without Jesus Christ? How can you live? Absolutely not possible. When Judas betrayed Jesus Christ for 30 dollars he died because he was separated from Jesus Christ who is life. We remember that when the devil was once the archangel, when he forgot God and said, "I am the creator," and then failed and separated from God who is life.

Also, when Adam lived peacefully in paradise for seven years and did what he was told not to do, he lost peace from God who is life, and found it difficult to live. but then we remember that he found peace when he returned to God, when he reconciled with God, so there is no peace without God.
 
Our questioner said that they want to die and live with Jesus Christ. So, those of us who do not have peace on earth, those who have fallen into sin on earth, those who have not tried to repent to find Jesus Christ, how can we find peace if we die? What qualifies us for the kingdom of heaven is the work we have done on earth to live with Jesus Christ and enable us to live in heaven. If we die on earth covered in sin, without repentance, confession, and reconciliation with God, we will not be able to live with Jesus. Therefore, it means that we cannot live with our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ before we repent.

text:
Our dear member told us that their mind is going to explode. It is God who gives us peace of mind. 
The mind wants shelter, it wants peace but the conscience blames it. For example, a person knows that stealing is bad before learning to steal, knows that killing is bad before learning to kill. Our consciousness tells us what is good and bad because that is the way it was created; Man is a creature created to distinguish good from evil, evil from good, and what is useful from what is not. 

Therefore, we must all seek life, and if we are willing to find life, we can repent of our sins and find God; God is near, God is love. "You return and I will return," God is not a cruel father who tells you to stay where you left. What He told us is  those of you who have fallen come back to me, . God is a compassionate and merciful father.
 
First He created us in His image, we humans failed to live, we fell, we were the kings of creation but because of our sin we fell from our glory; He came back in search of us, born of the Holy Virgin Mary as a man. After that, he paid many prices for us, to bring back our exiled ones, he was exiled for us, then He was whipped with 6666 lashes, crucified in the square of Calvary, to bring us back what we lost and even more. He gave us his holy body and his precious blood. Eat my flesh, drink my blood, that he may bring us back with food that we have fallen by eating, there is no greater life than this.

Even after He has conquered death,  He told us that  if you fall into sin, even if you make a mistake, repent and come to Me. Therefore, what is needed to live with God is to persevere in his house until the end, it is necessary to continuously take part of his holy body and his precious blood, the Eucharist. 
 
As we have said so far, life means living with God, and what is needed to live with God is to first repent. Therefore, may God help us all who have fallen into sin to repent, stay in the house until the end of our lives, receive His holy body and his precious blood, and live with God in his house.
 
Praise be to God, the Virgin Mother and the cross.

Today, we gather together to commemorate and celebrate the life and legacy of the esteemed Saint Yared of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Let us delve into the profound teachings and experiences of this great scholar and draw valuable lessons for our own spiritual journey.

text:
Born in the year 505 A.D., near the ancient city of Axum, Saint Yared's upbringing was marked by an early struggle to grasp education. As a young child, he faced difficulties in understanding his studies, which left him disheartened. His mind, however, was captivated by the love for the Virgin Mary and her divine Son. One fateful day, his teacher remarked that he lacked color, insinuating his inability to comprehend the lessons. When tested, young Yared failed to respond and was consequently beaten.

The pain of the punishment deeply affected him, prompting Saint Yared to distance himself from his teacher. Exhausted, he sought refuge in the Mai Kirah area and, in his weariness, received a divine revelation from God. The Lord taught him the importance of perseverance and unwavering effort. Encouraged by this divine guidance, Saint Yared returned to his teacher, sought forgiveness, and resumed his education with renewed determination. He diligently applied himself to his studies and devoted himself to prayer, seeking communion with God.

In His infinite mercy, God blessed Saint Yared with a profound spiritual experience through the intercession of the Virgin Mary. The mysteries that had previously eluded him were unveiled, and he received divine insights and understanding. During his prayers, when heavenly hyms had not yet been revealed, three angels, in the form of birds, appeared before him and spoke to him, granting him their divine counsel.

Reinvigorated by this encounter, Saint Yared returned to the earthly realm, filled with inspiration and gratitude. He offered his thanksgiving in Axum Zion, where the people and the king marveled at the depth and beauty of his spiritual compositions. Saint Yared served diligently in Axum and Debre Damo, ascending to higher spiritual heights with each passing day. Eventually, he left his homeland, aspiring to join the company of the Virgin Mary and the heavenly host.

Throughout the remainder of his life, Saint Yared authored five significant books, leaving a profound legacy for future generations. He established centers of learning and spiritual instruction in Tana Kirkos, Zur Amba, and other locations, where he nurtured and mentored numerous disciples. Saint Yared's contributions to Ethiopian Orthodox Church music are characterized by three distinct types of songs: Geez, Ezl, and Ararai.

The Geez songs, meaning "found first," represent liberation, reminding us of the freedom we find in Christ. The Ezl songs, comprising thirty melodies sung in conjunction with Geez or Tazlo Ezl, inspire fortitude and endurance in the face of trials. Lastly, the Ararai songs, characterized by a melancholic and tender melody, represent the Holy Spirit, who comforts and emboldens believers.
Within Saint Yared's musical compositions, we encounter various symbols that add depth and richness to the musical expression. The "Difat" (ድፋት) symbolizes the descent of Christ from heaven, encouraging us to humbly submit to God's will. The "Hidet" (ሂደት) symbol, exemplified by the Lord's earthly ministry, urges us to continue our journey without hindrance, following in His footsteps.
Furthermore, the "Kinat" (ቅናት) symbol instructs us to lift our heads and proclaim the truth boldly, just as Christ did when confronted by His accusers. The "Yizet" (ይዘት) symbol, observed when a song is read swiftly, reminds us of the Lord's arrest by the Jews. The "Kurt" (ቁርጥ) symbol calls for strength and resilience, likening it to Christ's decision to endure suffering for the redemption of humanity.

text:
👆🏾

We also encounter the "Chiret" (ጭረት) symbol, which denotes a quick movement within the melody, reflecting the urgency and swiftness of God's action. The "Rikrik" (ርክርክ) symbol encourages us to lengthen our spiritual melodies, reminding us of the eternal sacrifice of Christ and the abundant grace He bestows upon us. Lastly, the "Deret" (ደረት) symbol, characterized by a powerful and resounding voice, signifies the Lord's ascension, urging us to exalt and proclaim His glory.

Let us now explore some of the notable compositions of Saint Yared. "Dgwa,"(ድጓ) a song offered on Sundays and annual holidays, encompasses the Eucharistic celebration and conveys the profound mystery and joy of the Holy Communion. "Tsome Dgwa" (ጾመ ድጓ) refers to a specific variant of the song sung during the period of Abiy Lent, incorporating verses from Zawadah-Hosanna.
Another remarkable composition is "Zimare," (ዝማሬ) which is performed after the Eucharist. "Mwaset"(መዋሥዕት) is a prayer for the departed, sung during funerals, while "Mieraf" (ምዕራፍ) is a composition sung in every chapter, symbolizing a place of rest. The works of Saint Yared are intricate and carry profound spiritual significance, inviting us to explore the depths of our faith.
Saint Yared's spiritual journey continued as he traveled extensively, leaving an indelible mark on the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Saint Yared with his disciples Sawira, Eskender and Menker, embarked on a journey to the north, Semen Berh. They carried their hymn books and lived in the monastery by teaching hymns in the northern monastery. 

In one particularly extraordinary incident, Saint Yared entered the Axum Zion Church and placed his hands upon the sacred coffin. With a voice filled with reverence and awe, he uttered these words: "You are holy, you are blessed, you are praised; You are blessed. You are exalted, you are the ladder of light." As he recited his composition called "Anketse Berhan," (አንቀጸ ብርሃን) while singing the Ezl song, he ascended about an arm's length towards the heavens. This miraculous event left the psalmists astounded, and Saint Yared imparted his final words of guidance and farewell before retreating to a hidden cave, disappearing from this earthly realm.

On the 11th of May, in the year 571 A.D., at the age of 66, Saint Yared departed from this temporal existence, leaving behind a spiritual legacy that continues to inspire and uplift the faithful even to this day.

Dear brethren, as we reflect upon the life of Saint Yared, let us draw valuable lessons for our own spiritual journey. His unwavering commitment to education and perseverance in the face of challenges remind us of the importance of continuous learning and growth in our faith. Saint Yared's profound spiritual experiences and revelations underscore the transformative power of prayer and communion with God.

Through his hymnodical compositions and symbols, Saint Yared invites us to elevate our worship, allowing our voices and melodies to be a conduit for spiritual expression. His compositions, rich with deep meaning and divine inspiration, serve as a reminder of the beauty and majesty of our Orthodox tradition.

May we be inspired by the life and teachings of Saint Yared, remembering the importance of perseverance, unwavering faith, and an ardent pursuit of divine knowledge. Let us strive to cultivate a deep and vibrant spiritual life, expressing our devotion to God through worship and service. May Saint Yared's legacy continue to resonate within our hearts and guide us on our journey towards eternal communion with our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ. Amen.

text.text: Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, today is the monthly feast of St. Michael. Hence let us read the below text written about him and partake from his blessings.

text:
St. Michael, whose name echoes the divine query, "Who is like God?" stands as a beacon of divine strength and leadership. This mighty Archangel, esteemed in the heavenly hierarchy, is not merely a celestial being but also a symbol of hope and fortitude for the faithful. His role transcends the boundaries of heaven, extending his protective mantle over the faithful on earth.

Let us recall the ancient scriptures and the teachings of the Church Fathers, who spoke of St. Michael with reverence and awe. His presence in pivotal moments of Biblical history underscores his importance. When Joshua, leading the Israelites in the wilderness, encountered a divine figure with a drawn sword, it was none other than St. Michael, the captain of the Lord's host. This encounter, as narrated in the Book of Joshua, reveals the martial and protective aspects of St. Michael's character.

In the exodus from Egypt, where the Israelites were led from bondage to freedom, St. Michael was the guiding light, the angelic shepherd appointed by God Himself to safeguard His people. His role was not only as a guide but also as a guardian, ensuring the fulfillment of God's promises.

Furthermore, in the prophetic visions of Daniel, St. Michael emerges as a powerful intercessor and protector of the faithful. He is depicted as the great prince who stands guard over God's people, a testament to his enduring role in the salvation history.

In the New Testament, St. Michael's presence is equally profound. His role in the cosmic struggle against evil and his intercession for the faithful before the throne of God are themes that resonate throughout Christian theology.

The Orthodox Church, in its liturgical and theological tradition, has always held St. Michael in high esteem. His commemoration on the twelfth day of each month is not merely a ritualistic observance but a testament to his ongoing intercessory role. The Church teaches that St. Michael's prayers bring about the blessings of nature: the timely rains, the fruitful earth, the gentle winds—all are seen as manifestations of his intercession.

In our daily struggles and in the greater spiritual battle against sin and temptation, let us turn to St. Michael for guidance and protection. His example inspires us to stand firm in our faith, to confront the adversities of life with courage, and to remain steadfast in our devotion to God.

As we honor St. Michael, let us remember that his story is not just a tale from the past but a living reality that permeates the life of every Orthodox believer. In our prayers and in our actions, let us emulate his unwavering faith and his unceasing devotion to the will of God. May his intercession strengthen us, may his example guide us, and may his presence among us be a source of comfort and hope.

Thus, beloved in Christ, let us embrace the lessons and the legacy of the Archangel St. Michael. May his blessings be upon us, and may his intercession lead us closer to the divine. In his honor and memory, let us say, "Archangel Michael, pray for us, that we may be worthy of the promises of Christ." Amen.

text: The Orthodox Church firmly upholds the belief in the divinity of Jesus Christ. This belief is rooted in numerous scriptural references and is a cornerstone of Christian faith. The recognition of Jesus as God incarnate is not merely a theological concept but a profound truth that underpins the entirety of Christian doctrine and life.

:
 In John 1:1-14, the Scripture clearly states, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word becoming flesh and dwelling among us is the central mystery of the Christian faith. This incarnation is not just a divine visitation but God Himself entering into human history.

The resurrection of Christ is not just a testament to His power over death but also a confirmation of His divinity. As Paul writes in Romans 1:4, Jesus was "declared to be the Son of God with power according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead."
Christ's role as the Good Shepherd is a powerful image in Orthodox spirituality. It speaks of His loving and protective care for His flock, the Church.

In John 10:11, Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep." This is not just a metaphor but a reality that culminated in the crucifixion, where Christ sacrificed Himself for the redemption of humanity.
The image of Christ as a shepherd also symbolizes His guidance and protection. In the turmoil and challenges of life, Christ, the Good Shepherd, guides His flock towards salvation and peace.
The resurrection and ascension of Christ are central to Orthodox theology, symbolizing the defeat of death and the hope of eternal life.

Christ's resurrection is the triumph over death, not just His own, but for all who believe in Him. As Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:55-57, "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?"

The ascension of Christ, as witnessed in Acts 1:9-11, is not just a physical rising but a theological affirmation of His Lordship over all creation. It is a promise of His return and the establishment of His Kingdom in fullness.
The Orthodox understanding of judgment and salvation is deeply connected to the person and work of Jesus Christ.
In the Orthodox tradition, Christ is not only the Savior but also the Judge. As stated in 2 Corinthians 5:10, "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ."

Salvation in Orthodox theology is understood as a process of theosis, becoming partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). This process is made possible through Christ, who, being both fully God and fully man, bridges the gap between humanity and God.

It is essential to remember that the knowledge of Christ is not merely academic but transformative. The life, teachings, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ are not just historical events but realities that have a profound impact on our lives. As Orthodox Christians, we are called to live in the light of these truths, embodying the love, sacrifice, and hope that Christ Himself has shown us.

This exploration provides just a glimpse into the rich tapestry of Orthodox theology and Christology. It invites the reader to delve deeper into the mystery of Christ, a journey that leads to spiritual growth and a deeper understanding of the divine.

The Good Shepherd

2. Guidance and Protection:

2. The Ascension:

1. Christ as Judge:
In the Orthodox tradition, Christ is not only the Savior but also the Judge. As stated in 2 Corinthians 5:10, "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ."

2. Salvation through Christ:
Salvation in Orthodox theology is understood as a process of theosis, becoming partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). This process is made possible through Christ, who, being both fully God and fully man, bridges the gap between humanity and God.

text: The concept of a "Covenant of Mercy," deeply rooted in Orthodox theology, reflects the profound interplay between divine justice and mercy. This story, particularly centered around the Blessed Virgin Mary, is a vivid tapestry of faith, intercession, and divine promise, painting a picture of God's unending compassion towards humanity.

text.text: The Covenant with the Blessed Virgin Mary

text: The narrative of the Blessed Virgin Mary's covenant with Christ is a cornerstone of this theological understanding. In her plea at the tomb of Christ, Mary exemplifies the role of intercessor, a bridge between the divine and the human. Her plea, "My child, my friend... I am begging you to come and listen to my pleas," is not just a mother's cry but a symbolic representation of humanity's yearning for divine intervention and mercy.

At its core, the Covenant of Mercy is an oath, a divine promise of salvation and forgiveness. It transcends the boundaries of time and space, linking the faithful across generations. This covenant is not merely an agreement but an embodiment of God's unwavering commitment to His creation.

The concept of a covenant is deeply entrenched in the Scriptures. The Old Testament is replete with instances of covenants between God and His people, symbolizing a profound relationship based on commitments and promises. In the New Testament, this theme continues, particularly through the life and teachings of Jesus Christ, culminating in the New Covenant of grace and truth.

In Orthodox theology, saints hold a special place as intercessors and exemplars of divine grace. Their lives, a testament to faith and devotion, become channels through which God's mercy flows. The story of the covenant reminds us that the saints, in their earthly life and heavenly abode, continue to intercede for us, presenting our pleas before the throne of God.

### The Necessity of the Covenant

Why is such a covenant necessary? It stems from the inherent human condition marked by sin and frailty, as first seen in Adam. The covenant is God's response to this condition, offering a path to redemption and salvation. It is a beacon of hope, guiding the faithful towards a life of virtue and piety.

This covenant, however, is not a passive assurance. It calls for active participation in the form of good deeds. It is not an excuse for moral laxity but an encouragement to strive for righteousness, knowing that divine mercy is ever-present.

The mercy of God, as revealed in these narratives, is not limited to a select few but is a universal promise. It extends beyond the saints to every repentant sinner, offering forgiveness and a chance for renewal.

text.text: The Blessed Virgin Mary's Unique Role

text: In this celestial drama, the Blessed Virgin Mary holds a unique position. She is not only a recipient of this covenant but also an active participant in its dispensation. Her intercessory role is magnified in this covenant, making her a focal point of hope and salvation for all who seek her son, Jesus Christ.

In contemplating the "Story of the Covenant of Mercy," we are invited to reflect on the depth of God's love and the profound role of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the economy of salvation. This narrative is not just a historical account but a living reality that invites us to partake in the divine mercy, encouraging us to live lives worthy of this high calling.

In the spirit of John Chrysostom, let us ponder these truths, allowing them to transform our understanding and approach to our faith, leading us closer to the heart of God's unending mercy.

text: In the Orthodox understanding, stress is seen as a consequence of living in a fallen world. It is a manifestation of the brokenness that pervades human existence since the Fall. Stress arises from our daily struggles, whether they be physical, emotional, or spiritual. However, the Orthodox perspective does not view stress as merely a psychological or physical phenomenon but as a deeply spiritual one.

text.text: The Call to Trust in God

text: The central tenet of overcoming stress in Orthodox spirituality is absolute trust in God. This trust is beautifully encapsulated in the words of Jesus Christ, "Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life..." (Matthew 6:25). This exhortation is a call to remember that God, in His providence, cares for the smallest details of our lives. The Orthodox faithful are encouraged to believe that if God cares for the birds of the air, how much more will He care for His children made in His image (Matthew 6:26)?

text.text: The Role of Prayer and Faith

text: Prayer is a cornerstone in dealing with stress from an Orthodox viewpoint. Through prayer, believers cast their anxieties and worries upon God, as instructed by Apostle Peter, "casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7). Prayer is not seen merely as a request for help but as a means of communion with God, whereby the faithful align their wills with God's will, finding peace in His sovereign control over their lives.

Orthodox Christianity places great emphasis on the sacraments as a means of grace and healing. Participation in the Holy Eucharist, confession, and anointing with oil are seen as tangible means through which God imparts peace and healing to the stressed and anxious soul.

text.text: The Virtue of Patience and Endurance

text: The Orthodox tradition teaches that stress and suffering can be transformative when endured with patience and faith. St. Paul's words, "We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance..." (Romans 5:3), are a testament to this belief. Suffering and stress are not seen as mere obstacles but as opportunities for spiritual growth and deepening one's faith.

In times of stress, the Orthodox faithful also turn to the saints for intercession. The lives of the saints, who have endured great trials and tribulations, serve as a source of inspiration and comfort. The intercessions of the Theotokos (Mother of God) and other saints are sought, believing in their close communion with God and their ability to intercede on behalf of the faithful.

Orthodox spirituality also emphasizes the cultivation of inner peace through the practice of stillness (hesychasm). This involves quieting the mind and heart in the presence of God, often through the Jesus Prayer: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner." This practice helps to center the believer in God's presence, away from the tumult of external circumstances.

In the Orthodox understanding, stress is seen as a consequence of living in a fallen world. It is a manifestation of the brokenness that pervades human existence since the Fall. Stress arises from our daily struggles, whether they be physical, emotional, or spiritual. However, the Orthodox perspective does not view stress as merely a psychological or physical phenomenon but as a deeply spiritual one.

The Call to Trust in God

The central tenet of overcoming stress in Orthodox spirituality is absolute trust in God. This trust is beautifully encapsulated in the words of Jesus Christ, "Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life..." (Matthew 6:25). This exhortation is a call to remember that God, in His providence, cares for the smallest details of our lives. The Orthodox faithful are encouraged to believe that if God cares for the birds of the air, how much more will He care for His children made in His image (Matthew 6:26)?

The Role of Prayer and Faith

Prayer is a cornerstone in dealing with stress from an Orthodox viewpoint. Through prayer, believers cast their anxieties and worries upon God, as instructed by Apostle Peter, "casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7). Prayer is not seen merely as a request for help but as a means of communion with God, whereby the faithful align their wills with God's will, finding peace in His sovereign control over their lives.

The Sacramental Life

Orthodox Christianity places great emphasis on the sacraments as a means of grace and healing. Participation in the Holy Eucharist, confession, and anointing with oil are seen as tangible means through which God imparts peace and healing to the stressed and anxious soul.

The Virtue of Patience and Endurance

The Orthodox tradition teaches that stress and suffering can be transformative when endured with patience and faith. St. Paul's words, "We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance..." (Romans 5:3), are a testament to this belief. Suffering and stress are not seen as mere obstacles but as opportunities for spiritual growth and deepening one's faith.

In times of stress, the Orthodox faithful also turn to the saints for intercession. The lives of the saints, who have endured great trials and tribulations, serve as a source of inspiration and comfort. The intercessions of the Theotokos (Mother of God) and other saints are sought, believing in their close communion with God and their ability to intercede on behalf of the faithful.

This involves quieting the mind and heart in the presence of God, often through the Jesus Prayer: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner." This practice helps to center the believer in God's presence, away from the tumult of external circumstances.

In conclusion, the Orthodox approach to stress is holistic, addressing the spiritual, emotional, and physical aspects of a person. It emphasizes trust in God's providence, the power of prayer, the grace received through the sacraments, the transformative potential of suffering, the intercession of saints, and the cultivation of inner peace through stillness. text:
.

St. Gabriel is the 2nd ranked angel power after St. Michael among the 7 archangels. He is described in the scriptures equally as the Archangel Michael in his intercession and mediation. Gabriel means servant and messenger of God. He is given this mysterious name because it is often revealed in the form of a human being and conveys God's message or God's will to mankind. In the place where the angels were created, when God, who created them, disappeared from their eyes in an instant to ensure the stability of their religion. Then question arose in the society of angels: 'Who created us?', 'Where did we come from?'  At this time, the father of destruction, the devil, boldly and defiantly said, "I have created you." But the angel Saint Gabriel calmed down the association of countless holy angels by saying that we should stand firm where we are. Because of this, as it is written on John 1:14, 'The Word became flesh', he was chosen to announce to the Virgin that the Son of God  will come down from heaven and be born as a man from the Virgin Mary. The angel Gabriel said to the her, "Behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He is great. He will be called the Son of the Most High (Luke 1:31). Now that we have learned something about the Archangel, we will proceed with today's feast. 

This is the miracle he performed on December 28th (annual commemoration day) : Saint Gabriel saved the three men named Ananya, Azaria, and Misael (Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego) from the furnace fire. If you ask how this happened, when they were living in captivity in Persian Babylon, King Nebuchadnezzar made Daniel the fourth and placed them in the palace to learn wisdom from Babylon. Meldar, their steward, offered them meat and wine in goblets. They said, "We will not eat this. Give us some grain and good water." He said to them, "If the king sees your weight loss, he will be angry." They said give us a date. He gave them 10 days. They ate grains and drank water, and they were more handsome and bright than those who ate meat and drank wine. While they were learning, the Lord revealed his wisdom to them and they became wise, especially Daniel who enterpreted the king's vision. Then because of this, the king appointed them in three states. But the Babylonians were jealous of this and thought of a reason to quarrel with the king. They said to the king, make a picture of yourself so you can distinguish between your friend and your enemy. He made a gold statue 60 cubits high and 6 cubits wide and placed it in the field of Aduran and proclaimed that those who do not bow to it will be punished. When everybody bowed down, they  (Ananya, Azariah, and Mishael) said, "We will not bow down." And the Babylonians went and told the king. The king then ordered they be brought before him for questioning. He asked them 'Do you say that we should not worship?' They said yes. 'Who will save you?' They said to him "the God that created us will save us." He kindled a fire, and the flame became 49 cubits.

After this, he selected the mighty ones and threw the three into the fire. The soldiers who pushed them to fire were burned but  for the three (Ananya, Azariah, Misael) the angel Gabriel came down and touched the fire with his rod, it turned into water. When the Babylonians saw that the fire was extinguished, they added more fire to it and activated the burn. But they (Ananya, Azariah, Mishael) spent the night singing praises to God without being burned.

In the morning, when Nebuchadnezzar looked from his balcony, he saw four of them walking in the fire. 👉🏾 In addition to the above, here are some of the main works of intercession and mediation that the angel Saint Gabriel is known for, which he performed by the grace given to him from the Creator:-

👉 1st/ He told the prophet Daniel in a vision about what was going to happen. 15:16)

👉 2. Also, in the vision that the prophet Daniel saw again, he said this about the angel, "While I was still praying, the angel I had seen in the vision before, Gabriel, came flying... He taught me and told me... Daniel, I have come now to give you wisdom and understanding" (Dan 9: 21-23)

👉 3rd / Saint Gabriel is the angel who saved Daniel from the lion's mouth.

👉 4th /  Saint Gabriel saved the three men named Ananya, Azaria, and Misael from the furnace fire. 

👉 5th/ He announced to the priest Zacharias and Saint Elizabeth that they would give birth to John the Baptist in their old age.

👉 6. He announced to the Virgin Mary that the physical word Jesus Christ, who is the cure of the world, would be born from the her.

👉 7th/ He saved  St. Jeletan and the child Kirkos from a boiling fire in an iron tank. 

👉 8th/ He led the wise men to the city of Bethlehem where the Lord was born, leading them with the sign of a star.

👉 9th/ Old Joseph was told in a dream to take his mother and baby and flee to Egypt.

👉 10/ In addition, Saint Gabriel announced the conception of Samson; He brought forth water for Agar in the desert. He who interpreted the mystery to Daniel; He is an angel appointed over serpents and scorpions.

In general, we find this angel's intercession and guardianship in many readings of the holy books; God has helped us to write to you on the occasion of the monthly holiday that we celebrate today, March 28th, so that we may all receive the intercession and blessings of the angel Saint Gabriel. 

Therefore, if the Lord God had not sent his angels to protect us night and morning, day and night, on the road, when we sleep at home and when we get up, Satan's army would have prevent us from having life in this world and the next .

God's prophet, Saint David, said, "No calamity will enter your house. He will raise up angels for you to guard you on your way. They will lift you up with their hands so that your feet will not stumble over a stone..." Telling us about the guardianship and protection of angels.

In another paragraph, he said, "God's angel will live around those who fear him, and will save them." He said that angels will save people who believe in the guardianship and intercession of angels, and that they will save us from physical and spiritual suffering. (Ps 33:7, 90/91:10')

Since angels are appointed to have authority over all creatures, the prophet Enoch told us about the power of intercessor and guardianship of Saint Gabriel saying that he is one of the noble angels appointed over the serpents, the righteous in heaven, and the cherubim. (Enoch 6:7)

May the prayers and supplications of this great angel of light rest upon us

text:
My Beloved in Christ,

As we stand at the threshold of the New Year 2024, let us embrace it with a heart full of hope and a spirit eager for renewal. In the spirit of the Orthodox tradition, rather than a lengthy discourse, I offer you a simple yet profound lesson drawn from the depths of our faith.

Reflect upon the words of St. Paul in Ephesians 5:16, "Making the most of every opportunity, because the days are evil." This New Year, let us focus on the sacredness of time. Each moment is a precious gift from God, an opportunity for growth, for love, for repentance, and for deepening our communion with Him.

In our fast-paced, modern world, it is easy to become entangled in the transient and lose sight of the eternal. As an Orthodox Christian, strive to see each day as a chance to draw nearer to God. Engage in daily prayer, immerse yourself in the Holy Scriptures, and partake in the sacramental life of the Church. This is the path to true transformation.

Also, consider finding a spiritual father or mother. In the Orthodox tradition, a spiritual guide is invaluable for navigating the spiritual journey. They provide wisdom, encouragement, and a living example of Christ-like humility and love.

This New Year, let your resolution be to live each day in the presence of God, seeking His will and opening your heart to His transformative grace.

As you embark on this journey, ask yourself: "How can I make each day a step closer to God, making the most of the time He has blessed me with?"

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you in this New Year.

In Christ's Love.

text: Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, yesterday we celebrated the feast of the annunciation in the Ethiopian Orthodox church, hence we send you the following lesson so you can read and partake from the blessings of this wonderful event.

text.text: The Divine Announcement: A Cosmic Shift

text: In the Orthodox tradition, the Annunciation is not merely a historical event but a cosmic shift where heaven intersects with earth. The Archangel Gabriel's visitation to the Virgin Mary marks the beginning of humanity's salvation. This momentous occasion, celebrated with great reverence, signifies the initiation of the divine plan for redemption.

text.text: The Virgin Mary: The Fulcrum of Salvation

text: The Orthodox Church venerates the Virgin Mary, Theotokos, as the fulcrum of salvation history. Her response to Gabriel, "Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word" (Luke 1:38), encapsulates her humility, obedience, and faith. This assent is not passive but an active cooperation with God's grace. text: Dear members of John's Repentance spiritual service, today we send you a lesson on St. Tekle Haymanot, who's annual feast of nativity is celebrated today, so that you may better understand his story and use it as an inspiration to shape yours.

Just as a well-nurtured tree yields bounteous fruit, so too is the true faith enriched and passed down by holy servants of the Lord. Consider the chronicles of Saint Tekle Haymanot, the radiant beacon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

Born to the world on December 27, 1214 AD, his entry into this realm had been divinely announced the prior year, on March 27, 1214 AD. Originally christened "Fiseha Zion," he was reared under this name and in the devout shadow of his father, Tzaga Ze'ab. Young Fiseha Zion immersed himself in holy scriptures, the Bluyat and the Hadisat, manifesting an early zeal for divine matters. Legend recounts his prowess as a hunter, but in a profound epiphany, the heavens rent asunder, revealing our Savior Jesus Christ, borne on the wings of Archangel Michael, with a celestial chorus of angels in tow. Addressing the astounded youth, our Lord decreed, "Henceforth, you shall bear the name 'Planted Trinity,' and your hunt shall no longer be for game, but for souls. Fear not, for I am perpetually at your side." And then, as mysteriously as He had appeared, our Lord vanished into the heavenly expanse.

Armed with this divine mandate, Saint Tekle Haymanot distributed his earthly possessions among the needy and embarked on a divine mission, starting at Mnane. Ordained by the Pope, he began evangelizing with such enthusiasm that his very first sermon led ten thousand souls in the region of "Shwa Tsilalesh" to baptism. He then traversed vast tracts of Ethiopia, reclaiming lands and souls lost to foreign religions due to past onslaughts by Judith and Islamic influence. He unflinchingly faced down the heretical Marian sorcerers.

Apart from his evangelical conquests, Saint Tekle Haymanot was a cornerstone of monasticism in Ethiopia. His dedication saw him serve in three renowned monasteries: Abune Besilote Michael Monastery for twelve years, Abune Jesus Moa Zahaiq Monastery for seven years, and Debre Damo for another seven years alongside Abune Yohani. This sums up to an impressive twenty-six years. Post his monastic commitments, he retreated to Medreshwa (Zorre), where he spent twenty-two years in deep prayer, during which he famously planted six spears around him and prayed continuously for seven years.

His faith was not confined to Ethiopia. Spiritual encounters and blessings marked his pilgrimage to Jerusalem. At the sight of the sacred places, including Christ's crucifixion at Calvary, he wept bitterly. Legend speaks of a divine vision he received wherein he beheld the Holy Trinity in its unity and trinity and declared, "Glory to the Holy Trinity," before descending back to earth.

The miraculous exploits of Saint Tekle Haymanot are innumerable. He resurrected the dead, healed the ailing, exorcised demons, and performed wonders that transcended the earthly realm. He was a luminary, a beacon guiding many towards the light of Orthodoxy, and even founded Mount Lebanon Monastery, a unique abode where male and female monks coexisted in spiritual harmony. After a lifetime replete with tribulations and triumphs for the faith, he entered the heavenly abode at the age of ninety-nine, on August 25, 1314 AD.

text.text: May the blessings and intercession of our revered father, Saint Tekle Haymanot, always be our fortress and guide, amen.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every language that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of the Holy Mother of God, the Virgin, and the Cross be upon us. Amen.

text: Fasting, in the Orthodox understanding, transcends mere abstention from food. It is an act of obedience to God's command, a testament to the discipline of the soul over bodily desires. This practice traces its roots to the very beginning of human existence, as seen in the command given to Adam in the Garden of Eden. The abstention from certain foods was not merely a physical act but a spiritual exercise, teaching obedience, self-control, and dependence on God's wisdom and provision.

text.text: Fasting: A Path to Spiritual Liberation

text: The great fathers of the Church, like Mar Isaac, extolled fasting as the foundation of all spiritual endeavors. It is portrayed as the harbinger of virtues like purity, humility, and prayerfulness. Fasting is not only a means of controlling physical appetites but also a powerful tool for cleansing the soul, elevating the mind, and nurturing a heart attuned to the divine. It becomes a voluntary embrace of simplicity and a conscious rejection of worldly excesses.

The practice of fasting finds ample support in the Holy Scriptures. Christ Himself, following His baptism, retreated into the wilderness, engaging in a prolonged fast. This act set a precedent for His followers, illustrating the spiritual potency inherent in fasting. The prophets and apostles, following in the footsteps of Christ, embraced fasting as a means of reconciliation with God, a testament to its enduring spiritual significance.

text.text: The Theology of Fasting: A Means to God’s Grace

text: Fasting, in the Orthodox tradition, is intrinsically linked to the concept of grace. It is seen as a tangible expression of a believer's yearning for divine grace. The Fathers teach that fasting, combined with prayer, becomes a potent conduit for God's mercy, an instrument for the remission of sins, and a means of attaining spiritual insight. By subduing the physical, fasting elevates the spiritual, aligning the human will with the divine.

text.text: Fasting and the Conquest of Sin

text: In the Orthodox perspective, fasting is a powerful weapon in the battle against sin. It aids in purifying the heart and mind, allowing believers to focus more intently on God and His commandments. The practice serves as a bulwark against temptation, strengthening the believer's resolve to live in accordance with God's will.

text.text: Fasting: A Communal and Personal Discipline

text: While fasting is a deeply personal spiritual exercise, it also has a communal dimension in Orthodox Christianity. It fosters a sense of solidarity among believers, uniting them in their shared pursuit of spiritual growth and closeness to God. This communal aspect of fasting reinforces the concept of the Church as a body of believers journeying together towards salvation.

In an age marked by material excess and spiritual malaise, fasting emerges as a countercultural testament to the enduring relevance of spiritual disciplines. It offers a means of resistance against the pervasive influence of a consumerist society, inviting believers to seek fulfillment not in temporal pleasures but in the eternal joy of communion with God.

text.text: Conclusion: Embracing Fasting as a Way of Life

text: Fasting, as taught by the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and reflected in the eloquence of Church Fathers like John Chrysostom, is not merely an occasional religious observance. It is a way of life, a continual journey towards spiritual perfection, and a profound expression of love for God and neighbor. In embracing fasting, believers find not just spiritual discipline, but a path to the heart of the Christian faith – a journey of transformation, sanctification, and divine communion.

- It must be acknowledged that it leads to eternal life. "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day" (John 6:53).
 
- All those who partake of the Holy Communion must believe that Christ is with them, that they live together with Christ, that His flesh is united with their flesh, and their blood is united with His blood, and that their God is united with them by grace. (He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives with me, and I live in him" (John 6:56).

- It is necessary to repent from past sins, confess, return and guard against future sins. "After that John was put in prison, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God." (Mark 1:14) The Kingdom of God refers to His Holy Body and His Precious Blood.
 
- There is no age limit for receiving Holy Communion. From the day we were baptized on the 40th and 80th day after birth, where by we become being children of God and received the Holy Communion, we should not stay away from the Holy Communion since then until the end of our lives. It is a great mistake to think of youth as sinfulness in itself or a life unfit for the sacrament, and to think that we should  receive only in infancy and youth. There is no set age for approaching the Holy Communion and not approaching. The only thing that keeps us away from the Holy Communion is if we are highly involved in a particular sin and that we still do now and then being unable stop it. We should take a gap and and make sure to be committed to stop that particular sin first.  Unbelief should not be admitted to sin without repentance. "And now, says the Lord, return to me with all your hearts, fasting, weeping and wailing" (Acts 2:12).
 
 
- Husband and wife should receive Holy Communion together at the first time. If a husband and wife have not received the sacrament together before, it is not allowed for them to receive it separately or one side alone. But after they once received it together, they have already confirmed their unity in flesh and spirit, they can be receive separately. 
 
- In general, because our salvation Jesus Christ died for all, it is a wrong attitude to take the difference between married and single, race, color, sex and age. A person should live by receiving Holy Communion from his childhood until he gets married, when he gets married (together with his husband/wife), and after marriage until his death.
 
Points We  Need to know upon Preparation to receive Holy Communion
 
 
1.       Prepare with absolute faith. We should believe that what we receive is the holy body and precious blood of our Lord, who died on the cross of Calvary on Friday for the world's salvation. In addition, we should strengthned our belive saying to our self :- " I will find forgiveness through repentance for the sins I committed; I will find the strength to be protected from future sins, Christ is in me and I will live in Christ, I will find eternal salvation, I will be protected from a sick body and a sick soul." Saying this, we need to prepare with complete faith and always repent from sin before being anointed and prepare to receive it with faith.
 
(Part 2 to be continued)👇

text:
2.       If those receiving Holy Communion are married, they should abstain from sexual intercourse for 3 days before receiving Holy Communion. Sexual intercourse on permitted days in marriage is not a sin, but since it is an act of the flesh , so this period is also one of the forbidden days in terms of giving respect to the sacrament.
 
3.       Anyone who repents and is freed from his sins should keep his heart away from revenge and his body away from wrongdoing.

4.       In order to receive Holy Communion, one should fast for 18 hours without food and water, and wait until the feeling of food being removed from the stomach.

5.       If one sees inappropriate dreams, they will not receive Holy Communion that day. Also, if there is bleeding on anypart of a body, bleeding wound,  or if vomited, or if flys like a mosquito bite entered our the mouth or nose, it is not possible to receive on that day.

6. On the eve of the day we plan to receive Holy Communion, we should take a bath and clean what we wear.

7. Before starting the mass, it is necessary to attend the church and properly follow

the mass. We should be present before Liturgy starts, and ideally attend the services before that as well. 

8. A woman should  not receive until 7th days of her menstruation. Then she washes her body and can receives on the 8th day or after then. Also at the time of childbirth she does not receive it until he day of the Christening of the child. "If a woman gives birth, it means 80 days, if she gives birth to a boy, it means 40 days" (Leviticus 12:1-5)

text.text: Christ is born! Glory be to Him!

Beloved and respected members who follow the orthodox education and spiritual service that we convey on John's Repentance page, we send you this writing about today's feast, the nativity of Christ written by Bishop Youssef of the Coptic Orthodox Church because it is important to understand what we are celebrating, so we entrust you to read it and learn from it.

text:
The birth of our Lord Jesus Christ marks the beginning of a New Covenant between God and man, a covenant previously and purposefully foreshadowed and prepared for by a prior covenant.

In order to understand and appreciate the New Covenant that God has instituted with humanity, it is necessary to take a close look at the old one.

The Old Covenant was between God and Israel "And I will establish My covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you in their generations, for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and your descendants after you" (Genesis 17:7). The New Covenant, however, is established between God and any person who will receive the Son of God "But as many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God, to those who believe in His name who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:12,13).

The Old Covenant was temporary, and conditioned upon the Israelites’ obedience of the law. God foretold to Moses that this covenant would not last but would soon be broken, "this people will rise and play the harlot with the gods of the foreigners of the land, where they go to be among them, and they will forsake Me and break My covenant which I have made with them. Then My anger shall be aroused against them in that day, and I will forsake them" (Deut 31:16,17). On the other hand, the New Covenant is designed for eternal life; and will thus last forever. St. Paul says, "The God of peace who brought up our Lord Jesus from the dead, that great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant …" (Heb 13:20,21).

In the Old Covenant, there was no hope of eternal life for a person who broke any of the prescribed laws. In that sense, the law could not bring salvation nor justify anyone. All it could do was teach people the need for salvation by a Savior and by His grace granted henceforth. In contrast, in the New Testament, we are justified and sanctified by the work of our Lord Jesus Christ through the Holy Spirit.

The ceremony of the Old Covenant included the slaughter of a heifer, a goat, a ram, a dove, and a young pigeon. After that Abraham cut the carcasses in half, and then at sunset only God walked the blood path between the two pieces of the carcasses (Genesis 15). Usually both parties of the Covenant would walk the blood path between the slaughtered animals as a symbol of what would happen to either party if they violated the terms of the agreement. It is interesting to note that with Abraham, only God walked the blood path to indicate that if Abraham or his descendants dishonored the covenant, God and only God would have to pay the price with His own blood.

The New Covenant has been established not by the slaughter of animals but by the slaughter of the Son of God on the holy wood of the Cross, after having walked the blood path Himself. "Why is Your apparel red, And Your garments like one who treads in the winepress? I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with Me. For I have trodden them in My anger, And trampled them in My fury; Their blood is sprinkled upon My garments, and I have stained all My robes" (Isaiah 63:2-3).

Christ is born! Glory be to Him! 

Beloved and respected members who follow the orthodox education and spiritual service that we convey on John's Repentance page, we send you this writing about today's feast, the nativity of Christ written by Bishop Youssef of the Coptic Orthodox Church because it is important to understand what we are celebrating, so we entrust you to read it and learn from it.

"Why is Your apparel red, And Your garments like one who treads in the winepress? I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with Me. For I have trodden them in My anger, And trampled them in My fury; Their blood is sprinkled upon My garments, and I have stained all My robes" (Isaiah 63:2-3).

(To be continued) 👇🏾

text:
The old law revolved around a system of animal sacrifices performed by chosen priests from the tribe of Levi. These Levitical priests had to make an offering for their own sins before they could offer sacrifices on behalf of anyone else. It is important to note that, there were many priests, who because of their sins and consequent spiritual death were prevented from continually offering the sacrifice. On the other hand, in the New Covenant our Mediator is a High Priest who being sinless, offered His own blood (for our forgiveness) for us and brought His sacrifice to Heaven itself as the only perfect offering to God. Because He has been raised from the dead, His perfect priesthood continues forever (Heb 7:23,24).

While the Old Covenant was written on two tablets of stone, the New Covenant is an Internal Covenant written on our hearts by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us "I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts" (Heb 8:10).

We knew sin through the Law "the Old Covenant" (Rom 7:7-11) and with the Law, there was no forgiveness but curse and wrath. However, through the New Covenant we have received the forgiveness of our sins: "For I will be merciful to their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more" (Heb 8:12).

The Old Covenant revealed the holiness of God in the righteous standard of the Mosaic Law and promised the coming of the Redeemer, but the New Covenant has shown the holiness of God in the righteousness of His Son.

The Old Covenant became obsolete with the appearance of the New Covenant which is eternal: "When He said, ’A New Covenant,’ He has made the first obsolete. But whatever is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to disappear" (Heb 8:13).

From the above comparison between the old and new covenants, it is obvious that the New Covenant is a much better one because it establishes a new and better relationship between God and man… As St Paul says, "And for this reason He is the Mediator of the New covenant" (Heb9:15) because "… now He has obtained a more excellent ministry, inasmuch as He is also Mediator of a better covenant, which was established on better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, then no place would have been sought for a second" (Heb 8:6,7).

Through His incarnation, our Lord Jesus Christ became a Mediator of the New Covenant that was foreseen by Jeremiah the prophet, "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah--not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, My covenant which they broke, though I was a husband to them, says the Lord. But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put My law in their minds, and write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people. No more shall every man teach his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, 'Know the Lord,' for they all shall know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them, says the Lord. For I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin I will remember no more" (Jeremiah 31: 31-34).

St. John Chrysostom explains the meaning of a Mediator, "What is a 'Mediator'? A mediator is not lord of the thing of which he is mediator, but the thing belongs to one person, and the mediator is another: as for instance, the mediator of a marriage is not the bridegroom, but one who aids him who is about to be married. So then also here: The Son became Mediator between the Father and us. The Father willed not to leave us this inheritance, but was wroth against us, and was displeased with us as being estranged from Him; He accordingly became Mediator between us and Him, and prevailed with Him."

text:
👆🏾

The New Covenant has been instituted by the blood of the Lamb, "In the same manner He also took the cup after supper, saying, this cup is the new covenant in My blood. This do, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me" (1Cor 11:25). St. John Chrysostom elaborates, "But they were not sprinkled with "scarlet wool," nor yet "with hyssop." Why was this? Because the cleansing was not bodily but spiritual, and the blood was spiritual. How? It flowed not from the body of irrational animals, but from the Body prepared by the Spirit. With this blood not Moses but Christ sprinkled us, through the word which was spoken; "This is the blood of the New Testament, for the remission of sins." This word, instead of hyssop, having been dipped in the blood, sprinkles all. And there indeed the body was cleansed outwardly, for the purifying was bodily; but here, since the purifying is spiritual, it enters into the soul, and cleanses it, not being simply sprinkled over, but gushing forth in our souls. The initiated understand what is said. And in their case indeed one sprinkled just the surface; but he who was sprinkled washed it off again; for surely he did not go about continually stained with blood. But in the case of the soul it is not so, but the blood is mixed with its very substance, making it vigorous and pure, and leading it to the very unapproachable beauty."

Let us praise the Lord with the angels for His birth and the establishment of the New Covenant saying, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men."

May the Glorious Feast of the Nativity bless us and alert us to rededicate our hearts and lives to the New Covenant with our Lord Jesus Christ.

Bishop Youssef, 
              Coptic Orthodox
              Diocese of the Southern 
              United States

text.text: The Malady of Sin: A Soul's Sickness

text: In the Orthodox Christian understanding, sin is not merely a transgression of divine law but a profound sickness of the soul. Like a disease that ravages the body, sin corrodes our spiritual well-being, distancing us from God, who is the source of all life and health. This spiritual ailment manifests in our thoughts, actions, and the very orientation of our wills, leading us away from the divine harmony for which we were created.

text.text: Sin: A Severance from the Divine Will

text: Every sin, at its core, is a rebellion against the divine will, a deliberate turning away from the path God has ordained for us. This rebellion is not merely a legal infraction; it is a rupture in our relationship with our Creator, the source of all goodness and life. The gravity of sin lies in this separation, a severance from the life-giving communion with God.

Sin often masquerades as a false promise of fulfillment or freedom. It entices us with the allure of immediate gratification, blinding us to its long-term consequences. This deception leads us down a path of spiritual decay, where we become enslaved to our base passions and further estranged from our true purpose and identity in God.

text.text: The Call to Repentance and Transformation

text: In the Orthodox tradition, the antidote to sin is repentance — a radical reorientation of our lives towards God. This repentance is not merely a feeling of sorrow for wrongs committed; it is an active turning away from sin and a turning towards God. It involves a transformation of the heart and mind, a renewal of our inner selves according to the image of Christ.

text.text: The Sacramental Life: Healing for the Sin-Sick Soul

text: The Church, as the body of Christ, offers a path of healing through the sacraments. These sacred acts are not mere rituals; they are encounters with the living God who alone can restore our broken nature. In the sacrament of Confession, we bring our sins to light, receiving forgiveness and grace. In the Eucharist, we partake of the very life of Christ, who heals and transforms us from within.

text.text: The Struggle Against Sin: A Lifelong Journey

text: The Christian life is a constant struggle against sin. This struggle is not waged in our own strength but through the grace of God, which empowers and sustains us. We are called to vigilance, prayer, and ascetic discipline, always relying on the mercy and help of God to overcome the temptations and trials that beset us.

Despite the gravity of sin, the Orthodox faith is marked by a profound hope in the redeeming work of Christ. Through His life, death, and resurrection, Christ has conquered sin and death, offering us a path to restoration and eternal life. In Him, we find the promise of a renewed creation, where sin and its consequences are no more, and where we are fully united with God in a life of endless joy and peace.

In conclusion, from an Orthodox perspective, sin is a deep and pervasive problem that affects every aspect of our human existence. However, through the grace of God in Christ and the life of the Church, we are offered a path to healing and transformation. This journey requires our active participation in repentance, sacramental life, and the ongoing struggle against sin, always anchored in the hope of redemption through Christ.

messages.full_text:
👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾 Lesson about #Sin 

The Malady of Sin: A Soul's Sickness

In the Orthodox Christian understanding, sin is not merely a transgression of divine law but a profound sickness of the soul. Like a disease that ravages the body, sin corrodes our spiritual well-being, distancing us from God, who is the source of all life and health. This spiritual ailment manifests in our thoughts, actions, and the very orientation of our wills, leading us away from the divine harmony for which we were created.

Sin: A Severance from the Divine Will

Every sin, at its core, is a rebellion against the divine will, a deliberate turning away from the path God has ordained for us. This rebellion is not merely a legal infraction; it is a rupture in our relationship with our Creator, the source of all goodness and life. The gravity of sin lies in this separation, a severance from the life-giving communion with God.

The Deceptive Guise of Sin

Sin often masquerades as a false promise of fulfillment or freedom. It entices us with the allure of immediate gratification, blinding us to its long-term consequences. This deception leads us down a path of spiritual decay, where we become enslaved to our base passions and further estranged from our true purpose and identity in God.

The Call to Repentance and Transformation

In the Orthodox tradition, the antidote to sin is repentance — a radical reorientation of our lives towards God. This repentance is not merely a feeling of sorrow for wrongs committed; it is an active turning away from sin and a turning towards God. It involves a transformation of the heart and mind, a renewal of our inner selves according to the image of Christ.

The Sacramental Life: Healing for the Sin-Sick Soul

The Church, as the body of Christ, offers a path of healing through the sacraments. These sacred acts are not mere rituals; they are encounters with the living God who alone can restore our broken nature. In the sacrament of Confession, we bring our sins to light, receiving forgiveness and grace. In the Eucharist, we partake of the very life of Christ, who heals and transforms us from within.

The Struggle Against Sin: A Lifelong Journey

The Christian life is a constant struggle against sin. This struggle is not waged in our own strength but through the grace of God, which empowers and sustains us. We are called to vigilance, prayer, and ascetic discipline, always relying on the mercy and help of God to overcome the temptations and trials that beset us.

The Hope of Redemption

Despite the gravity of sin, the Orthodox faith is marked by a profound hope in the redeeming work of Christ. Through His life, death, and resurrection, Christ has conquered sin and death, offering us a path to restoration and eternal life. The life and teachings of St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus, a revered figure in Orthodox Christianity, offer a profound testament to the power of faith, asceticism, and divine intervention. His story begins in the land of Egypt, where his parents, Simeon and Aklesia, longed for a child for thirty years. In a miraculous occurrence, akin to the biblical stories of old, a divine voice promised them a son whose glory would surpass the heavens. This prophecy was fulfilled with the birth of Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus.

From his infancy, he exhibited signs of divine favor. His actions as a newborn, glorifying the Holy Trinity, and his angelic lifestyle, abstaining from earthly sustenance, marked him as a holy vessel. At the tender age of three, he was visited by Saint Gabriel, who brought blessings from the Virgin Mary and the celestial host. The Abbot Zemedeberhan, recognizing his sanctity, nurtured him in monastic life, where he flourished in spiritual wisdom and miraculous powers. His fame spread far and wide, leading to a pivotal moment when he healed a thousand blind men, a miracle reminiscent of Christ's own healings.

The spiritual journey of St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus was marked by profound solitude and communion with God. He was called to a life of seclusion in the forest, where his sustenance was of a heavenly nature, symbolic of man's reliance on divine grace rather than earthly provisions. His time in the wilderness was a testament to his unyielding faith and deep communion with God.

The saint's concern for humanity's salvation was paramount. His intercessions led to the liberation of souls from hell, showcasing his immense spiritual authority. His journey to Ethiopia, carried by Saint Gabriel, was a pivotal moment in his mission. There, he prayed fervently for the nation, an act of love and sacrifice, embodying the heart of a true shepherd.

St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus's life was not without trials. His encounter with Satan, who sought to hinder his mission, resulted in his temporary blindness. Yet, in this adversity, he was not forsaken; Saint Michael and Saint Gabriel came to his aid, a testimony to his favored status in the heavenly realms.

His ministry extended to Arabia, where he confronted idolatry and demonstrated the power of Christ through miraculous signs, converting many to Christianity. Even in the face of persecution, his faith remained unshaken, further attesting to his divine calling and steadfastness.

The life of St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus culminated in a glorious ascent, taken by angels to Jerusalem, where he was laid to rest. His earthly journey of 562 years, of which 262 was spent in Ethiopia, was marked by unwavering devotion, miraculous deeds, and a deep, transformative love for God and humanity.

This account of St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus, steeped in the traditions and teachings of Orthodox Christianity, serves as a beacon of spiritual guidance. His life exemplifies the virtues of faith, humility, and divine communion, offering a path to spiritual enlightenment and closeness to God. In his story, we find a profound reminder of the endless possibilities that faith in God can unlock, and the transformative power of living a life dedicated to divine service and love.
