text: What is the significance of the Tefisihee Mariam that the Deacons say in our church? For example: Antee Wi’itu mesobe werq qeyih ante wisteta mena biruh? I’ve said it myself, but I just don’t know what the importantance of it is in our faith?

Beloved in Christ, the query you have brought forth touches the heart of our liturgical tradition, reflecting the depth and beauty of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The Tefisihee Mariam, or the Praise of Mary, is a significant hymn chanted by deacons, lauding the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, for her pivotal role in the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. This hymn exemplifies our veneration of the Mother of God, not as a deity, but as the chosen vessel through whom God became man for our salvation. It embodies our acknowledgment of her virtues and her unique place in our salvation history.

The verse you're referring to "አንቲ ውእቱ መሶበ ወርቅ ንጹሕ እንተ ውስቴታ መና ኅቡዕ ኅብስት ዘወረደ አም ሰምያት ወሀቤ  ሕይወት ለኩኩ ዓለም," which translates to "Thou art the pot of pure gold wherein is hidden the manna, the bread which came down from heaven giving life unto all the world," beautifully articulates the Orthodox Christian belief in Mary as the Ark of the New Covenant. Just as the pot of manna in the Old Testament was kept in the Ark of the Covenant as a testament to God's provision for the Israelites in the desert, Mary is honored as the one who bore Christ, the true Manna from heaven, who gives eternal life to the world.

This verse draws us into the deep typology found in Scripture, where Mary is seen as fulfilling and surpassing the types and symbols of the Old Testament. The pure gold of the pot signifies her purity and the divine choice, while the hidden manna, Christ Himself, is the sustenance for our souls, the Bread of Life, who came down from heaven to nourish and redeem us.

Saint Cyril of Alexandria, a luminary father of the Church, beautifully expounds on this, saying, "Hail, Mary Theotokos, venerable treasure of the whole world... through whom the Holy Trinity is glorified and adored,... through whom the precious Cross is venerated throughout the world, through whom heaven exults, through whom angels and archangels rejoice, through whom demons are put to flight,... through whom the fallen creature is raised up to heaven, through whom the whole creation, possessed by idolatry, has come to the knowledge of the truth."

Thus, the Tefisihee Mariam is not merely a hymn of praise but a profound theological affirmation of the Incarnation and the central role of the Virgin Mary in our salvation. It invites us to marvel at the mystery of God's love and providence, drawing us closer to Him through veneration of His mother.

This understanding and reverence for the Virgin Mary are not mere traditions but are deeply rooted in the Scripture and the teachings of the Church Fathers. They invite us to ponder the mystery of our salvation and the extraordinary role that Mary plays in it, encouraging us to seek her intercessions and to emulate her faith and obedience to God's will.

As you reflect on this, consider how the understanding of Mary as the vessel containing the Bread of Life enriches your faith and draws you closer to Christ. How might this deepen your appreciation for the divine services and your personal devotion to the Theotokos?

Hello I have a question 

Why do we fast until 3pm? Is there a specific reason?

Beloved in Christ, the practice of fasting until 3pm is deeply rooted in the tradition of the Orthodox Church, reflecting our journey of self-denial, repentance, and communion with God. This specific time recalls the hour at which our Lord Jesus Christ gave up His spirit on the Cross for the salvation of the world, as noted in the Gospel of Matthew: "And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, 'Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?' that is, 'My God, My God, why have you forsaken me?'" (Matthew 27:46). By aligning our fast with this momentous hour, we unite ourselves more closely with the sufferings of Christ, remembering His ultimate sacrifice for us.

Fasting until 3pm allows us to exercise discipline over our physical desires, turning our focus towards spiritual nourishment and prayer. It is a tangible expression of our faith, reminding us to rely not on bread alone, "but on every word that comes from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4).

As you embark on this journey of fasting, consider how this practice might deepen your relationship with Christ. Reflect on the sacrifices He made for us and how we can offer our own small sacrifices as a way of drawing closer to Him. How might this period of fasting until 3pm enhance your spiritual life and lead you closer to the heart of God?

text.text: : A Reflection on the Third Week of the Great Lent

text:
In the heart of the Great Lent, there comes a week known by the faithful as Mekurab, translating from the ancient tongue as "Synagogue." This designation, while simple in its utterance, carries the weight of centuries, embodying the sacredness of worship and the solemnity of divine communion. It is within this week that the faithful are invited to journey deeper into the mystery of the Incarnation, where Christ Himself, the Word made flesh, enters into the synagogue, not merely as a participant, but as the very fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets.

The Synagogue, historically, stood as the gathering place of the faithful, where the Torah was read and God was worshipped in the beauty of holiness. It was in such a setting that our Lord often found Himself, teaching and revealing the depths of God’s love and commandments. The incident that marks the Mekurab week, as recalled in the sacred narrative, unfolds in the temple, where Christ, with righteous indignation, expels the merchants and money changers, proclaiming, "My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves." This act of purification is not merely an external cleansing of the physical space but an invitation to each soul to cleanse the temple of their own heart, making it a fitting abode for the Divine.

The Church, in her wisdom, has named the weeks of Lent, each carrying a profound spiritual theme that draws the faithful deeper into the mystery of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. Mekurab, or Synagogue week, thus becomes a focal point where the faithful are called to reflect on the sanctity of God’s house, both the historical temple and the temple of their own hearts, and to recommit themselves to making it a place of true worship, prayer, and divine encounter.

The liturgical life of this week is rich with scriptural readings and hymns that echo the themes of worship, divine zeal, and the call to righteous living. This Sunday's song from

"ቦአ ኢየሱስ ምኩራበ አይሁድ ወመሐረ ቃለ ሃይማኖት..." invites the faithful to contemplate the Lord's teaching in the synagogue, His preference for mercy over sacrifice, and His lordship over the Sabbath. This encapsulates the essence of the Mekurab week, inviting a meditation on how Christ fulfills and transcends the Law, embodying the true Sabbath rest for the souls of the faithful.

Saint Paul’s message to the Colossians, as read in this week, warns against being judged by external observances, reminding the faithful that the substance belongs to Christ. This calls for a deeper understanding that true worship transcends mere ritualistic compliance and finds its essence in the person of Christ. Similarly, the readings from the Epistle of James challenge the faithful to embody their faith through works of mercy and righteousness, reflecting the living faith that justifies.

The liturgical readings culminate in the Gospel narrative of Christ cleansing the temple, a powerful image of divine zeal and the call to purity. The faithful are reminded that the temple, Christ's Body, destroyed and raised up in three days, is the ultimate sign of God's presence and action among His people. Thus, the Mekurab week, through its liturgical and scriptural dimensions, invites the faithful to a profound encounter with Christ, the true Temple, where they are called to become living stones, built up into a spiritual house, offering spiritual sacrifices.

In this holy week of Mekurab, let the faithful be drawn into the heart of worship, where heaven and earth meet in the person of Christ. Let them cleanse the temples of their hearts, making room for the indwelling of the Spirit, and let their lives reflect the beauty of divine worship, not confined to the walls of any synagogue or temple but carried within the temple of the heart, sanctified by the presence of Christ, our Passover Lamb, who invites us all into the eternal Sabbath of His love and peace.

text: Was Jesus born in Ethiopia?

Beloved in Christ, grace to you and peace. Your question touches on the incarnate mystery of our Lord, Jesus Christ, who was born in Bethlehem, as foretold by the prophets of old. The Prophet Micah proclaimed, "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times" (Micah 5:2). This prophecy reveals the humility and divine plan of our Lord's nativity, not in Ethiopia, but in the land of Judea.

Ethiopia, however, holds a cherished place in Christian history, being one of the first nations to embrace the faith. The Ethiopian eunuch's baptism by Philip the Evangelist (Acts 8:26-40) signifies the spreading of the Gospel beyond the Jewish community, embracing all nations under the grace of Christ. This story is a testament to Ethiopia's early acceptance and devotion to the teachings of Christ, making it a beacon of faith from the earliest times.

text: Greetings again, I have another question. For me, being a Deacon is amazing. I feel like the Holy Spirit is dwelling with in me so much. I’m always intrigued to read the Holy Bible and to learn the Kidase. All though, I don’t know what a great blessing and significance being a Deacon truly is. Please explain to me the full history of Deaconhood and the history of the first Deacon who was known as St. Steven. Blessings, Goodnight.

Greetings in the peace of Christ,

The Diaconate is a sacred order, rich in history and spiritual significance, embodying service and dedication to the Church and to God’s people.

The role of a Deacon traces back to the early Church, as outlined in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 6. The Apostles, overwhelmed by their responsibilities, sought out seven men "of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom," (Acts 6:3) to assist in serving the widows and the needy. This marked the beginning of the Diaconate. Among these seven was Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit (Acts 6:5), who became the first martyr for Christ, bearing witness to the truth of the Gospel even unto death. His martyrdom highlights the depth of commitment and sacrifice inherent in serving God and His Church.

Being a Deacon, therefore, is not merely a role or a function; it is a vocation to embody the love and service of Christ, to minister to the faithful, and to be a living witness to the Gospel. It is a call to humility, service, and sometimes, sacrifice, as exemplified by St. Stephen. 

Your attraction to the Holy Scriptures and the Kidase (Divine Liturgy) is a foundation upon which your service is built, for through them, you encounter Christ and convey His presence to others. The significance of your role lies in this very act of service and witness, in the footsteps of Christ and His saints.

"Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be slave of all." (Mark 10:43-44)

Reflecting on the life and martyrdom of St. Stephen, how can you see your service as a Deacon being a reflection of Christ's service to the world?

text:
In the observance of Great Lent, the Church invites us to reflect on the profound narrative of the healing at Bethesda during its fourth week. This week, known as Metsague, derives its name from the story of a man who had been afflicted with illness for thirty-eight years, as recounted in the Gospel of John, chapter 5, verses 1 through 9. This narrative, rich in symbolism and divine truth, serves as a beacon of hope and a call to spiritual awakening, inviting us to delve deeper into the mysteries of faith, healing, and the boundless mercy of God.

In this poignant account, we encounter a figure, Metsague, who embodies the plight of humanity, ensnared by the frailties of the body and the desolation of the spirit. Bethesda, the place of this miraculous healing, with its five porticoes, becomes a symbol of the Church itself, a sanctuary for the ailing, the lost, and the forsaken, awaiting the stirring of the waters of grace. Here, the afflicted gathered, yearning for deliverance, for a touch of the divine that would transform their suffering into salvation.

It was amid this tableau of human misery that Jesus Christ, the Physician of our souls and bodies, approached Metsague. In asking, "Do you want to be healed?" Christ reveals a fundamental truth of our spiritual journey—the necessity of our consent in the work of our own salvation. The man's response, marked by despair and resignation, echoes the condition of many souls who, though desiring deliverance, find themselves paralyzed by their infirmities, unable to reach the healing waters by their own strength.

In commanding Metsague to rise, take up his bed, and walk, Christ demonstrates His authority over sin and death, over all that binds humanity in chains of despair. This act of healing on the Sabbath, which aroused the ire of the legalistic observers, underscores the Lord's message that mercy triumphs over judgment, that the law of love supersedes the letter of the law. Through this miracle, Christ invites us to a Sabbath rest in Him, to find in His mercy and love the true healing of our souls.

Metsague's healing is not merely a historical event but a living testament to the ongoing work of Christ in the world. It beckons us to recognize our own infirmities, our own pools of Bethesda, where we lie in wait for the stirring of the waters. It challenges us to hear Christ's call to rise from our slumber of sin and despair, to embrace the cross of self-denial, and to walk in the newness of life that He offers.

As we journey through the third week of Great Lent, let us meditate upon the profound symbolism of Metsague's healing. Let us contemplate the depth of Christ's mercy, which seeks us out in our infirmities, asking each of us, "Do you want to be healed?" May our hearts respond with a fervent "Yes, Lord," trusting in His power to transform our lives, to bear our infirmities, and to guide us to the still waters of His peace.

In this time of solemn reflection, let us also remember that, like Metsague, we are called to be witnesses to the miracle of grace in our lives, to carry our bed of suffering and follow Christ with resolute faith. For in our healing, we are called not only to salvation but to bear witness to the glory of God, to become beacons of hope and instruments of His mercy in a world yearning for redemption.

May the story of Metsague inspire us to deeper faith, to a more profound understanding of our own need for healing, and to a renewed commitment to follow Christ, our Savior and Healer, through the arduous path of Lent to the glorious dawn of Resurrection.

text:
What does the church advise about careers that consume a lot of your time & potentially limit the amount of time you can spend in church service & activities ? 

For example if i want to become a doctor, the education process will keep me busy and limit the time i can spend in service. In addition, when i start working as a doctor it will be the same. Would this be considered okay as long as i strive to live a sacramental life and serve God with the time I have. Or would the church recommend carefully considering the careers we choose with respect to how that affects our service life. 

Thank you 🙏🏾

Dear beloved in Christ,

Your inquiry touches upon a fundamental aspect of our journey with the Lord, where the balance between worldly duties and spiritual commitments often presents a challenge. The Orthodox Church, deeply rooted in the wisdom of the Holy Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers, offers a perspective that transcends the apparent dichotomy between secular occupations and spiritual life.

Saint Paul reminds us in Colossians 3:23, "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men." This verse encapsulates the essence of the Christian approach to work and vocation. The Church does not discourage us from pursuing careers, such as in medicine, that demand a significant portion of our time. Rather, it encourages us to see our professions as arenas for serving Christ and manifesting His love. Being a doctor, you are provided with unique opportunities to serve Christ in the sick and the suffering, embodying the healing ministry of our Lord Jesus.

The key is to ensure that your career does not lead you away from your ultimate goal—the salvation of your soul and union with Christ. It is indeed possible to lead a sacramental life and serve God with the time you have, integrating your faith into your daily work. The challenge is to maintain a prayerful life and participate in the Church's sacraments as much as your circumstances allow.

Consider the words of St. John Chrysostom, who taught that every aspect of our lives could be an offering to God if done in a spirit of love and dedication to His glory. Your career as a doctor, fueled by compassion and the desire to alleviate suffering, can be a powerful ministry and a path to sanctity.

Reflecting on how to balance your career and spiritual life, ask yourself: How can I make my work an offering to God? What steps can I take to ensure that my profession strengthens rather than diminishes my relationship with Christ?

In serving others through your profession, you serve Christ Himself. What will be your first step to integrating your faith with your work, making your life a living testimony of God’s love and mercy?

text:
This feast, which we celebrate today, is rooted deeply in the ethos of our faith, and beckons us to a profound reflection on the Crucifixion, a pivotal moment where divinity intersects with humanity in an act of unparalleled love and redemption.

The narrative of the Crucifixion, as we have inherited through sacred tradition and the Gospel of John, unfolds in the shadow of Gethsemane. It was there, amidst the olive groves, where the tranquility of the night was pierced by the approach of those who sought to capture Jesus of Nazareth. His response, imbued with divine authority, "I am he," caused them to stagger and fall—a testament to the power of His presence and the depth of His willingness to embrace His fate.

This encounter underlines a profound truth: the Crucifixion was not an event borne out of vulnerability or defeat but a conscious sacrifice, chosen by the one who commands the stars and treads upon the waters. In this divine paradox, we find the essence of our faith—the Almighty, bound; the Creator, subjected to His creation; the Giver of Life, embracing death.

As the events of that fateful day unfolded, our Lord, adorned not with regal gold but with a crown of thorns, reveals the heart of God's kingdom: one not of earthly power but of sacrificial love. Mocked and scorned, bearing a cross that symbolized not only His suffering but the weight of humanity's sin, He advanced towards Golgotha. With each step, the reality of His mission became clearer—to reconcile the world unto Himself, transforming an instrument of torture into the beacon of hope.

Upon the hill where Adam's sin cast a long shadow, the New Adam was lifted high. Nailed to the cross, His outstretched arms gathered the expanse of human frailty, offering it up to the Father in an act of ultimate intercession. It was here, at Calvary, that the fountain of mercy was opened, washing away the stains of sin and bridging the chasm wrought by our transgressions.

The cruelty of His tormentors, the indifference of the onlookers, and the tears of the faithful formed the backdrop to this cosmic drama. Yet, beyond the physical torment—a number so vast it numbs the mind—was the spiritual anguish of the Son, forsaken, that the world might be redeemed.

This yearly feast of Medhanialem is not merely a historical remembrance but a living participation in the mystery of the Cross. It invites us to enter into the paradox of Christian life: that in dying we find life, in surrender, victory, and in suffering, joy. As we reflect on the Crucifixion, let us also look beyond, to the Resurrection, where the fullness of God's promise is realized, and the hope of glory shines undimmed.

May the remembrance of Jesus Christ's suffering, His cross, death, and resurrection, not only recall the depths from which we have been lifted but inspire us to live lives worthy of the calling we have received. In this holy contemplation, let us draw near to the heart of God, finding in His wounds our healing, in His death our life, and in His love the strength to carry our crosses with faith, hope, and love. Amen.

is a spiritual bridge through which man can connect with God.

is a spiritual tool to defeat our enemy Satan.
is a special application that we ask for strength from the living God.
is a thanksgiving to God.
is a way we promise to God secretly that we will do legacy work once our prayer is answered.

is a way for a person to communicate with the Creator through his religion, thanking the Creator and begging for the forgiveness of sins. There is no wall that can prevent Him from hearing our prayers as long as we repent, do His will, and call upon Him with faith and a broken heart. The main skill to have in prayer is a broken heart, which includes: a broken heart, a broken spirit, tears, being humble and  refraining from revenge.

is a special tool through which we communicate with God. For this, we only need a broken heart, and we are not required to have a special speech style like we do when talking to a person. Nor do we have to explain the matter from beginning to end as He knows what we need more than we do. (Romans 1:27) If we speak to him with a pure heart, at any moment, God will listen to our prayers. God doesn't say, "I can't talk to you now, come back another time." He is always near to hear us the moment we come to talk to him.
 
In fact, the basis of prayer is the word of God:

text.text: "Ask and it will be given to you, seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened to you." (

text:
Matthew 7:7) Prayer is one of the rituals commanded by God. It includes worship, supplication, repentance, intercession, worship, love, vows and forgiveness.
 
As written in Genesis 2:7, God created man and breathed into him the breath of life through his mouth, and he became a living soul.  This living soul thirsts for God. The means for this is prayer. In the prayer, there is religion or believing and trusting. As St. John the Baptist taught us the art of prayer, a person who knows how to communicate with God and communicates with God in the right way will become like an angel from that moment on. No matter how noble or slave or ordinary or lowly or even a king a person is,  this is how the soul is freed from the shackles of the flesh, this is how the conscience is elevated, this is how our abode crosses to heaven, this is how a person despises worldly conduct, this is how one stands before the throne. Through a proper way of Prayer. For God does not look at the beauty of speech or the eloquence of words, but the purity of the spirit. Even if we come with a broken and pure heart and faith, and say what comes to our mind, we will get reply. It is said that "Your heavenly Father knows what you need without asking."
 
After all, the main purpose of prayer is communion with God, so there is no ritual without prayer. In every liturgy there is prayer. It can be said that all the good deeds that people do are prayers. Fathers and scholars say that prostration, almsgiving, repentance, pursuing spiritual education, etc. are classified as prayer. Therefore, when we say that a person prayed, we understand that he begged, thanked, sang, promised, repented, and talked with God. It is inevitable that human beings will offer thanks and praise to the God whom they worship: saying feed me, protect me  from evil and suffering.

(Continues) 👇🏾

We have mentioned that prayer is a special spiritual tool to connect with God. For this to happen, our relationship with God must be continuous and constant. We should adhere to God's commandments and observe fasts in religion and morals. Psalm 2:11 “Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling” 

What does it mean to fear the Lord ? Are we supposed to be scared or is it about having respect / reverence. Or is it the type of fear where we know our lives and destiny is in His hands and how we should do good in fear so we don’t end up in hell?

Beloved in Christ, your inquiry touches upon a profound aspect of our spiritual journey—understanding the fear of the Lord. In the Orthodox tradition, this concept is not about terror or dread, but rather a deep reverence and awe for God, acknowledging His infinite holiness and majesty. It is the beginning of wisdom, as Solomon the Wise proclaims in Proverbs 9:10, "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding." This fear is a form of love, a recognition of God’s omnipotence and our desire to live in harmony with His will.

It is indeed a respectful fear, one that compels us to turn away from sin and embrace a life of virtue, not out of terror of punishment, but out of love and a desire not to grieve our Heavenly Father. It’s a call to remember that our actions in this life echo into eternity, shaping our relationship with the Divine.

This reverence is nurtured through prayer, participation in the sacraments, and living a life in accordance with the teachings of Christ and His Church. It is about cultivating a heart that is sensitive to the presence of God in all aspects of our lives, leading us to act justly and love mercy.

As you contemplate this reverence for the Lord, ask yourself: How can I cultivate a deeper sense of awe and love for God in my daily life? How might this reverent fear guide me to live in closer communion with Him and His creation?

How does a person commitment their life to God & choose Him over the world? 

What does a person who has submitted His life to God look like?

Beloved in Christ,

Your inquiry touches the very essence of our journey towards the Kingdom of Heaven. To commit one's life to God and choose Him over the world is to embark on a path of transformation, guided by faith, prayer, and the Sacraments of the Church.

The Scripture illuminates this path in Matthew 6:33, "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and His righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you." This verse encapsulates the heart of commitment to God: prioritizing His will above all earthly concerns, trusting that He will provide for your needs.

A person who has submitted his life to God is often recognized by the fruits of the Spirit manifest in their life, as outlined in Galatians 5:22-23 — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. These qualities emerge not from human effort alone but through cooperation with the grace of God, allowing His Spirit to transform us from within.

Engaging in regular prayer, fasting, partaking of the Holy Eucharist, and confession are not mere rituals but means of grace, helping us to draw nearer to God and detach from worldly desires. Through these practices, guided by a spiritual father or mother, we learn to discern God's voice and His will for our lives.

Remember, dear one, that this journey is not a solitary endeavor. The Church offers us a community of faith, a spiritual family, to support and uplift us as we walk this path together.

Now, I ask you, what step will you take today to draw closer to God and seek His kingdom above all else?

text:
In the quiet sanctity of the Lenten season, as the world draws closer to the solemnity of Holy Week, the Church turns its contemplation toward the Mount of Olives, a site of immense spiritual significance, not only for its historical ties to the final days of our Lord Jesus Christ on Earth but as a beacon that illumines the profound mysteries of His second coming. In this hallowed week, termed "Mount of Olives" in the liturgical calendar, we are invited to meditate on the eschatological events that shall precede and encompass the return of Christ, the Judge of all, in glory and majesty.

As the sun sets over the ancient city of Jerusalem, casting elongated shadows from the olive trees, our minds are transported back to that pivotal moment when Christ, seated on this very mount, imparted to His disciples the knowledge of the end times, intertwining warnings with promises, terror with hope. It is a scene charged with the gravity of impending judgment, yet radiant with the promise of ultimate redemption for the faithful.

The imagery employed to depict the second coming is both vivid and veiled, a tapestry woven from the threads of divine revelation and human apprehension. Christ's return will be heralded by signs that eclipse the splendors and terrors of nature: a day when the celestial bodies falter in their courses, when the very elements seem to unravel, heralding the advent of the King of kings. The dead, both great and small, shall rise from their graves in a resurrection that knows no distinction of status or wealth, for in that moment, all humanity stands equal before the throne of God. The books shall be opened, those tomes of divine justice, wherein every deed, word, and thought are inscribed, awaiting the unfailing judgment of the Almighty.

This scene of judgment, as revealed through sacred scripture and tradition, transcends mere metaphor. It is a divine mystery that penetrates the core of our being, urging us to a life of holiness and vigilance. The Mount of Olives discourse serves not merely as a prophetic forecast but as a moral compass, guiding the faithful through the tempests of temporal life toward the harbor of eternal salvation.

The parable of the sheep and the goats, as recounted by Christ, encapsulates the essence of divine judgment. It is a delineation of destiny based not on the capriciousness of fate but on the concrete realities of moral choices and actions. The righteous, likened to sheep, are those who have embodied the virtues of the Gospel, extending love, compassion, and mercy to the least of their brethren. Their reward is a share in the eternal kingdom, a realm where suffering, sorrow, and death no longer hold sway. Conversely, the wicked, represented by goats, are those who turned away from the light of divine love, ensnared by the illusions of sin and selfishness. Their lot is separation from the source of all goodness, an exile as profound as it is self-imposed.

Yet, amidst these reflections on judgment and destiny, the Church, following the example of Christ, calls not for despair but for hope and transformation. The Lenten journey, especially as it converges upon the week of the Mount of Olives, is an invitation to introspection, repentance, and renewal. It is a time to shed the garments of sin that shroud the soul, to embrace the light of Christ that seeks to illumine every heart.

In this sacred season, let us then ascend in spirit to the Mount of Olives, there to keep watch with Christ in the garden of our hearts. May we be found vigilant in faith, steadfast in hope, and abounding in love when the Son of Man comes in His glory, accompanied by all His angels. Let us pray that, by His grace, we may be counted among the righteous, who will inherit the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world, where tears are wiped away, and joy is everlasting.

text:
Hello. What is the significance and importance of the Gate of Light for the praises of St. Mary? What is the significance and importance of the Malk of St. Mary and the Malk of Jesus?

Answer፦ Greetings in the peace of Christ. Your inquiry touches upon profound aspects of our faith that elevate the heart to God through the veneration of His saints, notably the Theotokos, St. Mary.

The "Gate of Light" within the context of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church refers to a liturgical hymn, part of the larger corpus sung during the midnight praises in honor of St. Mary. This hymn illuminates her role as the gate through which the True Light, Christ, entered into the world. As proclaimed in the Gospel of John, "The true light that gives light to everyone was coming into the world" (John 1:9). This hymn, therefore, emphasizes the Theotokos as a pivotal figure in our salvation history through whom divine grace entered into our temporal condition.

Regarding the "Malk of St. Mary" and the "Malk of Jesus," these refer to the respective praises and services dedicated to St. Mary and Jesus. In the tradition of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, a "Malk" is a spiritual song or service of praise. The Malk of St. Mary involves prayers, hymns, and readings that extol her virtues and her role in the mystery of the Incarnation. The Malk of Jesus, similarly, is focused on Christ Himself, praising His divine actions and His human life, from His miraculous birth to His redemptive Passion. These services deepen our connection to the divine through the veneration of Mary, who is always pointing us to her Son, and to Christ Himself as our Savior.

These practices are not just acts of devotion but are deeply transformative, guiding the faithful towards a life reflective of Christ's love and Mary's obedience. Engaging with these praises allows one to enter into a spiritual rhythm that sanctifies time and elevates the soul towards God.

Now, dear questioner, how might you incorporate these beautiful traditions of praise into your daily walk with Christ to deepen your faith and draw nearer to the Light of the World?

text:
፦ 1) Can girls drink Holy water when they are on their period? & why are they not allowed to go inside the church? 

2) Is labor pain related to the curse after the fall?

Greetings in the love of our Lord,

Your questions touch on significant aspects of our faith and tradition, which illuminate the profound wisdom of the Orthodox Church.

1) In Orthodox tradition, all faithful, regardless of their physical condition, can partake of Holy Water. Holy Water, blessed by the grace of God, is for the healing of soul and body and does not discriminate based on natural bodily processes. As for attending the Church, traditional customs vary, but the essence lies in the preparation and state of one’s heart. In some traditions, women refrain from receiving Communion during their menstrual period, a practice rooted more in historical cultural contexts than in doctrinal necessity. The important thing is the attitude of prayer and reverence towards the sacred mysteries.

St. John Chrysostom once said, "It is not the place that adorns the person, but the person that adorns the place." (Homilies on the Statues, Homily XX) The focus should always be on our inner disposition and our relationship with God.

2) Concerning labor pains, indeed, they are related to the narrative of the fall in Genesis. The Scriptures tell us, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children" (Genesis 3:16). This passage reflects the consequences of the original sin affecting humanity, including the introduction of pain in childbirth. Yet, in every suffering, there is a potential for spiritual growth and deeper reliance on God's grace. Pain, when united with Christ’s suffering, can become a source of spiritual strength and renewal.

As you continue to reflect on these aspects of our faith, consider how the practices and teachings of the Orthodox Church can guide you to a deeper relationship with Christ. What steps will you take to deepen your understanding and experience of our faith?

Beloved and respected, all our members who follow the orthodox education that we convey on John's Repentance page; Based on the questions on the topic above, we have sent you the important lesson below, so we entrust you all to read and learn from it.
About the Holy Communion, its Origin and the ceremony

text:
According to the canon of our Church, the Holy Eucharist (Qurban) is one of the seven sacraments of the Church. Qurban is a Surist and Greek (Arabic) word that means blessing, gift of money, knowledge, labor and time. In the Old Testament, the blood of animals offered by the Israelites for their sins and for the glory of God was called a sacrifice.
 
In the Old Testament era, the blood of animals offered by the Israelites for their sins and for the glory of God was called 'sacrifice', 'communion'.

text.text: But in the New Testament, communion or sacrifice means the faithful (true) sacrifice that God offered as an offering to reconcile himself with mankind. Therefore, the sacrament means the perfect body and blood of our God, Jesus Christ, our Savior, the Lamb of God.
It is our God, our Savior, Jesus Christ, who founded the sacrament of the Holy Communion

text: . And the day he started the system is the eve of the crucifixion on Thursday. When our savior established this great system and secret, only his twelve disciples were with him, and he did not reveal it to all the people who were following him as before. This is the reason why the Church still presents it with a veil and honor. When our Lord was sacrificed on the cross, in order to cover Him, the sun was dark the moon was covered with blood and the stars dropped down like withered fruit like chilies .

text.text: Even the angels of heaven dare not touch the sacrifice, for this is given only to the priests.
The Holy Communion is called a mystery

text: . Our Lord Jesus Christ took the bread, blessed it, consecrated it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, "This is my flesh." About the Holy Communion, its Origin and the ceremony

According to the canon of our Church, the Holy Eucharist (Qurban) is one of the seven sacraments of the Church. Qurban is a Surist and Greek (Arabic) word that means blessing, gift of money, knowledge, labor and time. In the Old Testament, the blood of animals offered by the Israelites for their sins and for the glory of God was called a sacrifice.
 
In the Old Testament era, the blood of animals offered by the Israelites for their sins and for the glory of God was called 'sacrifice', 'communion'.
 
But in the New Testament, communion or sacrifice means the faithful (true) sacrifice that God offered as an offering to reconcile himself with mankind. Therefore, the sacrament means the perfect body and blood of our God, Jesus Christ, our Savior, the Lamb of God.

It is our God, our Savior, Jesus Christ, who founded the sacrament of the Holy Communion. And the day he started the system is the eve of the crucifixion on Thursday. When our savior established this great system and secret, only his twelve disciples were with him, and he did not reveal it to all the people who were following him as before. This is the reason why the Church still presents it with a veil and honor. When our Lord was sacrificed on the cross, in order to cover Him, the sun was dark the moon was covered with blood and the stars dropped down like withered fruit like chilies . Even the angels of heaven dare not touch the sacrifice, for this is given only to the priests.
 
The Holy Communion is called a mystery. Our Lord Jesus Christ took the bread, blessed it, consecrated it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, "This is my flesh." I wanted to ask another culture-centered question if you don't mind. How come I hear a huge emphasis on what the faithful should do after taking the Eucharist? It's so emphasized I have had a priest tell me it's a sin for me to break these rules that requires confession

Example of Rules:
1. Don't touch water
2. Don't spit
3. You cannot sweat or play
4. You cannot cry
etc.

In the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the guidelines and traditions following the reception of the Holy Eucharist are deeply embedded in our liturgical and spiritual life, emphasizing the sanctity of the sacrament.

When an Ethiopian Orthodox Christian partakes of the Holy Eucharist, it is believed that they receive Christ Himself. Given the profound holiness of this act, the faithful are taught to remain in a state of purity post-communion as long as the Body and Blood of Christ are present within them. The guidelines you mentioned—such as not touching water, not spitting, avoiding physical exertion, and not crying—are cultural practices specific to Ethiopian Orthodoxy, designed to honor the presence of Christ within us and to avoid any act that might seem to expel or disrespect the Holy Gifts.

These practices are not ends in themselves but are disciplines that help the faithful to maintain a prayerful and contemplative state after receiving the Eucharist. They serve to cultivate a deep, ongoing awareness of God's immediate presence and to extend the sacredness of the liturgical experience into daily life. As St. John Chrysostom teaches, "Let us return from that Table like lions breathing out fire, having become terrible to the devil, thinking of our Head [Christ] and the love He has shown for us... This Blood makes the image of our King to be freshly painted in us, produces beauty unspeakable, permits not the beauty to fade, but refreshes it continually, when it is about to be destroyed."

However, it's crucial to understand that the Church's canonical law does not specifically prescribe these as absolute requirements; rather, they are traditions that have been upheld by the faithful over centuries. It is essential for those who find these practices burdensome or confusing to speak with their spiritual father. A spiritual guide can provide personalized guidance and help distinguish between essential ecclesiastical mandates and beneficial cultural traditions.

Given your interest in these practices, might I suggest further exploring how they might enhance your reverence and love for the Eucharist, guiding you to a deeper communion with our Lord Jesus Christ? What ways do you feel called to honor this sacred gift in your daily walk with Christ?

Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, as we dwell upon the teachings of the fifth week of Lent, known reverently as Guebre Hère, let us immerse ourselves in the profound insights of the Parable of the Talents, as rendered in the Gospel according to Saint Matthew, chapter 25, verses 14 through 30. This parable, bestowed upon us by our Lord Jesus Christ, is a beacon of spiritual guidance, particularly during this penitential season.

In this sacred parable, a man, about to journey afar, entrusts his property to his servants. To one he grants five talents, to another two, and to another one, each according to his unique ability. Upon his return, he assesses what has been achieved with his assets. The servants who received five and two talents respectively, engage diligently in their tasks, each doubling what was entrusted to them, and are thus richly praised and rewarded: "Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master." The servant who received one talent, however, out of fear, conceals his talent in the earth and is severely reproached and expelled into the darkness.

From this narrative, essential truths unfold:

The master distributes talents in alignment with the servant's abilities, mirroring how our Heavenly Father endows us with spiritual gifts tailored to our capacities. Each of us is given specific talents, meticulously aligned with divine intent and purpose, as Saint Paul articulates in his letter to the Corinthians.

The expectation of the master that the talents be not merely preserved but augmented underscores our duty to enhance and amplify the gifts bestowed upon us. These gifts, both spiritual and temporal, are granted not for idleness but for active and fruitful multiplication in God’s service.

The master’s return and settlement of accounts with his servants highlight the unavoidable truth of divine judgment. Each of us must live with the awareness that we shall stand before God to account for our stewardship, urging us to live each day with zeal and commitment to His divine will.

The master’s generous commendation of the faithful servants exemplifies God's boundless grace towards those who labor earnestly in His vineyard. The joy promised by the master symbolizes the eternal happiness that awaits the righteous, a reward infinitely surpassing earthly pleasures.

The chastisement of the servant who hid his talent is a stern admonition against negligence and fear. We are called to act boldly, employing our talents in the propagation of faith and spiritual advancement, rather than succumbing to fear or complacency.

Let us, therefore, brothers and sisters, draw inspiration from the essence of Guebre Hère, the exemplar who maximized the potential of what was entrusted to him. Let us introspect on our own talents, whether they be of spiritual insight, material means, intellectual acumen, or relational capacities, and consider how we might employ these gifts for the greater glory of God and the betterment of humanity.

May this contemplation on the Parable of the Talents embolden us to be like Guebre Hère, wisely and vigorously investing in the gifts we have received. Let us shun the path of the fearful servant and aspire to hear those blessed words from our Lord, "Well done, good and faithful servant... Enter into the joy of your master."

In this sacred season of reflection, may our hearts be stirred to fuller dedication and purpose, ever mindful of the watchful gaze of our Savior, who measures our faithfulness in the stewardship of His gifts. For it is in these faithful endeavors that we sow the seeds of our eternal felicity in the kingdom of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ. Amen.

I never thought about it like that 🤔. The rules seems very forced upon the laity that it seems legalistic, removing the freedom the honor the gift individually.

I guess I would want to 2 more questions:
1. Could you dive into the dietary restrictions in Ethiopia? Ive also been told its a sin to not follow the restrictions 

2. How do we as a Church balance culture and Orthodoxy? I've seen too often where culture has been enforced as a legalistic weapon rather than a freedom of expression. But I also know that culture is also a means of unity in a community. What are your thoughts?

Dear Nathan,

Your reflections bring to light the essential tension between tradition and personal spiritual freedom—a core concern for many in their journey of faith. Let's explore your questions one by one.

1.

:
   In Ethiopian Orthodox practice, dietary rules are primarily observed during fasting periods, which are numerous throughout the year, including prominent fasts such as the Great Lent, the Apostles' Fast, the Assumption Fast, and the Advent Fast. During these times, the faithful abstain from all animal products, including meat, dairy, and eggs, adhering instead to a vegan diet. This discipline is seen not merely as dietary but as a spiritual exercise to strengthen one’s spirit by the voluntary weakening of the flesh.

   These fasting rules are deeply rooted in Scripture and tradition. As Genesis 2:17 teaches, “But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.” This passage underlines the idea of abstaining for the sake of spiritual health. It is important, however, to recognize that while the Church prescribes these fasts for the spiritual benefit of the community, individual circumstances such as health, age, and life situation (e.g., pregnancy, travel) can necessitate adjustments, which should be discussed with one's spiritual father.

2.

:
   The interplay between culture and faith is indeed profound. Culture can both enrich and challenge the practice of Orthodoxy. The key to balancing them lies in discernment and the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Cultural practices become problematic when they overshadow the core doctrines of the faith or impose unnecessary burdens on the faithful. As the Apostle Paul instructs us, "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient" (1 Corinthians 6:12). This principle guides us to embrace cultural expressions that uplift and unite the faithful in Christ while being wary of those that may lead to division or spiritual harm.

   In practice, this balance is achieved through the living tradition of the Church—its liturgical life, canonical regulations, and the pastoral guidance provided by its bishops and priests, who are tasked with interpreting these in light of the Gospel. A healthy community life in the Church often reflects a harmonious blend where culture serves the higher goals of the faith, promoting a unity that does not stifle individual expression but rather celebrates it within the framework of Orthodox life.

Your insightful questions suggest a deepening engagement with these aspects of our faith. How might you continue to explore these intersections in your own life, and how can this exploration enhance your spiritual growth and participation in the community?

Question፦ I never thought about it like that 🤔. The rules seems very forced upon the laity that it seems legalistic, removing the freedom the honor the gift individually.

I guess I would want to 2 more questions:
1. Could you dive into the dietary restrictions in Ethiopia? Ive also been told its a sin to not follow the restrictions 

2. How do we as a Church balance culture and Orthodoxy? I've seen too often where culture has been enforced as a legalistic weapon rather than a freedom of expression. But I also know that culture is also a means of unity in a community. What are your thoughts?

Answer፦ Dear Nathan,

Your reflections bring to light the essential tension between tradition and personal spiritual freedom—a core concern for many in their journey of faith. Let's explore your questions one by one.

1. Dietary Restrictions in Ethiopian Orthodoxy:
   In Ethiopian Orthodox practice, dietary rules are primarily observed during fasting periods, which are numerous throughout the year, including prominent fasts such as the Great Lent, the Apostles' Fast, the Assumption Fast, and the Advent Fast. During these times, the faithful abstain from all animal products, including meat, dairy, and eggs, adhering instead to a vegan diet. This discipline is seen not merely as dietary but as a spiritual exercise to strengthen one’s spirit by the voluntary weakening of the flesh.

   These fasting rules are deeply rooted in Scripture and tradition. As Genesis 2:17 teaches, “But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.” This passage underlines the idea of abstaining for the sake of spiritual health. It is important, however, to recognize that while the Church prescribes these fasts for the spiritual benefit of the community, individual circumstances such as health, age, and life situation (e.g., pregnancy, travel) can necessitate adjustments, which should be discussed with one's spiritual father.

2. Balancing Culture and Orthodoxy:
   The interplay between culture and faith is indeed profound. Culture can both enrich and challenge the practice of Orthodoxy. The key to balancing them lies in discernment and the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Cultural practices become problematic when they overshadow the core doctrines of the faith or impose unnecessary burdens on the faithful. As the Apostle Paul instructs us, "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient" (1 Corinthians 6:12). This principle guides us to embrace cultural expressions that uplift and unite the faithful in Christ while being wary of those that may lead to division or spiritual harm.

   In practice, this balance is achieved through the living tradition of the Church—its liturgical life, canonical regulations, and the pastoral guidance provided by its bishops and priests, who are tasked with interpreting these in light of the Gospel. A healthy community life in the Church often reflects a harmonious blend where culture serves the higher goals of the faith, promoting a unity that does not stifle individual expression but rather celebrates it within the framework of Orthodox life.

Your insightful questions suggest a deepening engagement with these aspects of our faith. How might you continue to explore these intersections in your own life, and how can this exploration enhance your spiritual growth and participation in the community?

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

Also, my previous priest would tell me it was a sin to break the post Eucharist cultural traditions (such as touching water) and was something I needed to confess. If our spiritual father mistakes cultural traditions as doctrines or dogmas, is that perhaps a sign to get another spiritual father that is perhaps more knowledgeable about Orthodoxy?

👉

Dear Nathan,

Your concerns about the boundaries between cultural traditions and ecclesiastical doctrine are very valid and reflect a desire for a pure and undiluted practice of Orthodoxy. The role of a spiritual father is indeed pivotal, providing guidance and interpretation of the Church's teachings and traditions. It is crucial that this guidance be deeply rooted in the authentic teaching and spiritual wisdom of the Church.

If you find that certain practices, particularly those that are culturally rather than doctrinally based, are being enforced as if they were dogmatic or doctrinal requirements, it is important to seek clarification. The Church, in its wisdom, differentiates between tradition (which can be culturally specific) and dogma (which is universally applicable and doctrinally sound). When cultural traditions are mistakenly presented as dogma, it can lead to confusion and spiritual burden.

Approaching your spiritual father for a dialogue is a recommended first step. Express your concerns respectfully and ask for clarification on the teachings. If after such discussions, you continue to feel that the guidance you are receiving does not align with the broader, universal teachings of Orthodoxy, or it leads to spiritual distress rather than growth, it may be appropriate to seek additional perspectives. Consulting with another knowledgeable and experienced clergy member can provide a broader understanding and help affirm whether your spiritual concerns are being adequately addressed.

The relationship with a spiritual father should be one that fosters spiritual growth, understanding, and a deeper connection with the teachings of the Church. If you consistently feel that your spiritual needs and quest for Orthodox truth are not being met, it may indeed be prudent to consider finding a spiritual guide who can better support your journey.

text.text: : The Seventh Week of Great Lent

text:
.This week, often referred to by the Orthodox Tewahedo Church as "Nicodemus," is an opportune time to delve into the spiritual and theological implications of his encounters with Christ as detailed in the Gospel of John.

Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin, appears thrice in the Gospel of John, signifying stages of his spiritual journey and enlightening us on the path of true discipleship. His nocturnal visit to Jesus, as recounted in John 3, opens a profound dialogue on rebirth and the Kingdom of God, revealing the depth of Nicodemus's inquiry and his yearning for truth amidst a time of great religious complexity and expectation.

The night, often a symbol of obscurity and confusion in biblical texts, here illustrates the initial spiritual condition of Nicodemus—a man shrouded in the darkness of incomplete understanding yet seeking the light of Christ’s wisdom. His approach to Jesus under cover of darkness signifies not only a literal but a metaphorical seeking: an exploration from the shadows of ritual and law into the luminosity of grace and truth.

text.text: Rebirth and the Kingdom of God

text: In his dialogue with Jesus, Nicodemus grapples with the concept of being "born again," a fundamental tenet for any who wish to see the kingdom of God. This discourse is not merely doctrinal but deeply transformative, as it challenges the very paradigms through which Nicodemus has understood the world. Jesus’s explanation of spiritual rebirth—as essential as it is mysterious—highlights the transformative power of the Holy Spirit, who, like the wind, moves invisibly and unpredictably, conferring new life to those born of water and Spirit.

The subsequent mentions of Nicodemus in John 7 and John 19 show a man in transition, moving from cautious curiosity to a more courageous, albeit discreet, discipleship. In John 7, Nicodemus defends Jesus’ right to a fair hearing under the law, risking his reputation amongst his peers. By John 19, he assists in Jesus’ burial, an act of quiet defiance and devotion, signaling his embrace of the path of discipleship, regardless of its cost.

text.text: The Journey from Darkness to Light

text: : Nicodemus’s journey encourages the faithful to move from the shadows of ritual compliance and societal expectation into the transformative light of personal spiritual experience. It teaches us that faith is not static but dynamic, evolving from questioning to understanding, from hearing to doing.

: Despite his high status and the potential for significant personal loss, Nicodemus shows us the importance of seeking truth, even when it means standing alone. This courage to challenge prevailing orthodoxies and embrace new teachings is pivotal for personal spiritual growth.

: Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, submits himself as a student in the spiritual kingdom where Jesus is the master. His example reminds us that true wisdom often begins with the acknowledgment of what we do not know, and that humility is a vessel for divine revelation.

text.text: 4. The Witness to Faith through Actions

text:
: The actions of Nicodemus, especially in the burial of Christ, demonstrate that true faith is not merely professed but practiced. In risking defilement and disgrace to give Jesus a proper burial, Nicodemus embodies the sacrificial nature of love and loyalty that characterizes genuine discipleship.

As we reflect on Nicodemus this Lent, let us consider our own journey towards Christ. Are we seekers of truth, willing to step out from the comfort of our understandings and positions to learn anew at the feet of Jesus? Are we ready to be born again, not just of water, but of the Spirit, to enter into a life transformed by divine grace?

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾 Lesson on #Nicodemus: The Seventh Week of Great Lent

.This week, often referred to by the Orthodox Tewahedo Church as "Nicodemus," is an opportune time to delve into the spiritual and theological implications of his encounters with Christ as detailed in the Gospel of John.

Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin, appears thrice in the Gospel of John, signifying stages of his spiritual journey and enlightening us on the path of true discipleship. His nocturnal visit to Jesus, as recounted in John 3, opens a profound dialogue on rebirth and the Kingdom of God, revealing the depth of Nicodemus's inquiry and his yearning for truth amidst a time of great religious complexity and expectation.

The Context of Nicodemus's Inquiry

The night, often a symbol of obscurity and confusion in biblical texts, here illustrates the initial spiritual condition of Nicodemus—a man shrouded in the darkness of incomplete understanding yet seeking the light of Christ’s wisdom. His approach to Jesus under cover of darkness signifies not only a literal but a metaphorical seeking: an exploration from the shadows of ritual and law into the luminosity of grace and truth.

Rebirth and the Kingdom of God

In his dialogue with Jesus, Nicodemus grapples with the concept of being "born again," a fundamental tenet for any who wish to see the kingdom of God. This discourse is not merely doctrinal but deeply transformative, as it challenges the very paradigms through which Nicodemus has understood the world. Jesus’s explanation of spiritual rebirth—as essential as it is mysterious—highlights the transformative power of the Holy Spirit, who, like the wind, moves invisibly and unpredictably, conferring new life to those born of water and Spirit.

The Development of Faith

The subsequent mentions of Nicodemus in John 7 and John 19 show a man in transition, moving from cautious curiosity to a more courageous, albeit discreet, discipleship. In John 7, Nicodemus defends Jesus’ right to a fair hearing under the law, risking his reputation amongst his peers. By John 19, he assists in Jesus’ burial, an act of quiet defiance and devotion, signaling his embrace of the path of discipleship, regardless of its cost.

Spiritual Implications for the Faithful

1. The Journey from Darkness to Light: Nicodemus’s journey encourages the faithful to move from the shadows of ritual compliance and societal expectation into the transformative light of personal spiritual experience. It teaches us that faith is not static but dynamic, evolving from questioning to understanding, from hearing to doing.

2. The Courage to Seek Truth: Despite his high status and the potential for significant personal loss, Nicodemus shows us the importance of seeking truth, even when it means standing alone. This courage to challenge prevailing orthodoxies and embrace new teachings is pivotal for personal spiritual growth.

3.The Humility to Learn and Grow: Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, submits himself as a student in the spiritual kingdom where Jesus is the master. His example reminds us that true wisdom often begins with the acknowledgment of what we do not know, and that humility is a vessel for divine revelation.

4. The Witness to Faith through Actions: The actions of Nicodemus, especially in the burial of Christ, demonstrate that true faith is not merely professed but practiced. In risking defilement and disgrace to give Jesus a proper burial, Nicodemus embodies the sacrificial nature of love and loyalty that characterizes genuine discipleship.

As we reflect on Nicodemus this Lent, let us consider our own journey towards Christ. Are we seekers of truth, willing to step out from the comfort of our understandings and positions to learn anew at the feet of Jesus? Are we ready to be born again, not just of water, but of the Spirit, to enter into a life transformed by divine grace?

Can you explain how to apply these Bible teachings in daily life:

1. What does being "the salt of the earth" mean in practical terms?
2. Does removing the log from our own eye before judging others mean we should first address our own faults?
3. Does "the measure you give will be the measure you get" suggest that our judgments will be reciprocated?
4. What does striving for God's Kingdom and His righteousness involve, and what should we expect from it?
5. In what way should we ask, knock, and seek in our relationship with God?
6. How can we identify false prophets or insincere people by their "fruits"? 

Could you help clarify these concepts?

Dear seeker of truth,

Your inquiry into these profound scriptures is a commendable pursuit toward deepening your understanding and spiritual growth. Let us explore these verses in light of the Church's teachings.

1.

: In Matthew 5:13, Christ calls His followers to be "the salt of the earth." This metaphor signifies the indispensable Christian duty to enhance and preserve the moral integrity of the world. If the salt loses its flavor, it symbolizes losing one's spiritual zeal and virtue, becoming ineffective in our Christian witness. Saint John Chrysostom explains this as a dire warning to maintain the strength of our faith and virtue, lest we fail our purpose and are "thrown out and trampled."

2.

text.text: Removing the Log from Your Own Eye

text:
: The verse from Matthew 7:5 indeed suggests that we must first address our own sins and failings before correcting others. This is more than just a practical self-improvement; it is a profound spiritual principle of humility and self-awareness. It reminds us to approach others with compassion rather than judgment, recognizing our own imperfections.

3.

: In Matthew 7:2, the principle that "with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged" reflects the divine justice that mirrors our own attitudes and actions back to us. It is not akin to karma in its traditional sense but rather a biblical principle that God's judgment upon us corresponds to how we judge others.

4.

: Matthew 6:33's call to "strive first for the kingdom of God and His righteousness" is indeed about aligning our lives with God's commandments and embracing a life of virtue. Practically, this means living out the virtues you mentioned—honesty, purity, and faithfulness—trusting that God will provide for our needs according to His will and in His time.

5.

: These actions in Matthew 7:7 highlight the importance of persistent and active faith. We must not only ask but also seek and knock, showing our commitment and effort in pursuing the things of God. It is a progressive deepening of engagement with God and His promises.

6.

: Finally, in Matthew 7:15-20, discerning "by their fruits" is crucial in evaluating the true character of others, particularly those who claim spiritual authority. True spiritual life manifests in observable virtues—love, joy, peace, and the like. Those consistently exhibiting negative behaviors ("bad fruits") reveal a heart not aligned with God’s ways.

In all these, the overarching theme is that our faith must be lived actively and consciously, reflecting inwardly in our actions and outwardly through our interactions with others. In Orthodoxy, this life is best supported through a relationship with a spiritual father or guide who can help nurture these virtues in us.

What step will you take today to align more closely with these teachings of Christ? May the peace of the Lord guide you on this path.

text.text: Respected and beloved John's repentant website members, who follow the Orthodox lesson and spiritual counsel  which we serve to provide in a daily basis; It is to be recalled that, we sent a series of sections on the basic points on the subject. Today, we have sent you the next part as follows, so we entrust you all to read and learn from it.

text:
1.       A person who is not present when the Liturgy begins or who doesn't follow it thoroughly by being present for the whole service is not allowed to receive the Eucharist. Likewise, a priest cannot serve in Liturgy if he isn't present before it starts. Therefore, when we plan to receive the Eucharist, we should make sure to arrive at the church before the Liturgy begins.

2.       It is necessary to focus our thoughts on the Liturgy, approach in fear of God, and most importantly, we should approach in an absolute belief to get salvation for our body and soul in the Holy Eucharist

3.       If you know the prayer to be prayed when you receive Holy Communion, you should say it in heart, or else, we should approach it in the fear of God by thinking repeatedly in our hearts that this is the flesh and blood of Christ. In the same way, when receiving it, you should say 'Amen' once on the body and twice on the blood. (Mass Apostles)

4.       According to the order of the Church, from the bishops to the deacons, to the faithful, everyone receives the Holy Communion in line according to their rank.

5.       Once after receiving the Holy flesh and blood of Jesus Christ, you should drink Holy water. This holy water is served right there for those who received Eucharist, and it represents the water that flowed from our Lord's right side while he was pierced by a spear as he was on the cross.  Then, you should cover your mouth because it helps to remember that we shouldn't discuss earthly things before we eat something (Fit Men 13 Krista 65).

6.       If possible, it is preferable for the receiver of Holy Communion to be accompanied by someone.  But this is not an obligation or a law written by the church, but from the point of view of having someone by his side to help facilitating things so that he does not face challenges. 

8.       Those who do not believe and didn't take lesson about the Holy Communion are forbidden to receive it. So, it is necessary to monitor and control this.  (Ft Men 23 Rasub 44) They should first get a lesson from their church teachers or from their father of repetance about the Mystrery of communion in advance and believe that the sacrament they receive is the flesh and blood of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

9.       If a penitent person falls ill with a fatal illness before completing the period of penance, he is not prevented from receiving the Eucharist. On the other hand, a person who is in the canon of penance cannot receive Holy Communion without finishing the canon he received, unless he is in a life-threatening illness.
 
10.   A person who is tormented by a demon, a sick person, is not prevented from receiving Holy Eucharist. (Ft Men 13)

This holy water is served right there for those who received Eucharist, and it represents the water that flowed from our Lord's right side while he was pierced by a spear as he was on the cross.  Then, you should cover your mouth because it helps to remember that we shouldn't discuss earthly things before we eat something (Fit Men 13 Krista 65).

6.       If possible, it is preferable for the receiver of Holy Communion to be accompanied by someone.  But this is not an obligation or a law written by the church, but from the point of view of having someone by his side to help facilitating things so that he does not face challenges. 

8.       Those who do not believe and didn't take lesson about the Holy Communion are forbidden to receive it. So, it is necessary to monitor and control this.  (Ft Men 23 Rasub 44) They should first get a lesson from their church teachers or from their father of repetance about the Mystrery of communion in advance and believe that the sacrament they receive is the flesh and blood of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

9.       If a penitent person falls ill with a fatal illness before completing the period of penance, he is not prevented from receiving the Eucharist. On the other hand, a person who is in the canon of penance cannot receive Holy Communion without finishing the canon he received, unless he is in a life-threatening illness.
 
10.   A person who is tormented by a demon, a sick person, is not prevented from receiving Holy Eucharist. (Ft Men 13)

text.text: The precautions a Christian should take on the day he receives Holy Communion, and the Christian life he should have in his future life:

text:
1.       On the day a Christian receives Holy Communion, he should not wash his body with water, he should not take off his clothes and be naked, he should not draw blood from his body.
 
2.        He should not do hard work that can cause fluid (sweat) on our body, he should not walk a long way (because this is also considered work).
 
3.       Even if we live in a married life, it is necessary to abstain from sexual intercourse 3 days before receiving Holy Communion and 2 days after receiving Holy Communion. 
 
4.       He should not eat too much, drink intoxicating drinks that disturb what we have eaten and drunk.
 
5.       On the day we received Holy Communion, it is forbidden to cut nails, shave hair, bow and kneel, spit, bathe in water, and change clothes before the end of the day. (Liturgy No. 166) We can change our cloths at the evening after 6:00pm, as it is considered as the next day.

6.       if a person experiences nose bleeding , vomit, bodily bleeding, wounds, and a gnat that enters his mouth by Being careless or due to not taking appropriate care on the day of receiving the Holy Communion,  he should tell this to his penitent  father and  he should repent. And he cannot receive the Holy Communion again without performing his penance.  
 
7.       It is forbidden to go to Court and argue on the day you receive Holy Communion. (Council of Nicaea) In general, one should not go to a public place where there is an argument, argue with someone, talk with hard words, do work that provokes anger, and such other things after communion on that day.
 

8.       Before we receive Holy Communion, we should ask for forgiveness and be cleared of our sins of enmitity and revenge through repetance; and promise not to return back on it. So, now after receiving Holy Communion, we should refreain by far from argument, dispute and grudge. We should  be more committed to stay back from being offended, rebuked, or quarreled with. Even if it happens being out of control, we should ask for forgiveness, let go of grudges, repent and accept it as it should be. Be it from your family or social life, you should stay away from this type of situation as much as possible and spend everything patiently so that you don't have ideas that bring resentment and quarrels. We should live in love with everyone.
 
9.       After receiving Holy Communion, we should refrain from any sinful activity, such as adultery, murder, theft, gossip, addiction, fraud, lying, and the like. 
 
10.   After receiving Holy Communion, it is appropriate to listen to the word of God, go to church regularly, pray, fast, prostrate, and generally live a spiritual life and Christian behavior.

11.   It is necessary for us to have a regular prayer program in our personal life. Because the main spiritual struggle that we can do is through prayer so that Satan does not fight and deprive us of the blessings we have received through the Holy Communion.
 
12.   In general, it is appropriate to know that when we live bounded by the Holy Communion, it is never appropriate to go to a place that is contrary to spiritual life and to associate with a situation that exposes us to sin. We should fight against all the evil temptations and sin.

(Continues) 👇🏾

text.text: The Precautions and Christian Life a Believer Should Follow Before and After Receiving Holy Communion.

text:
Holy Communion signifies a commitment to follow the Orthodox Church's teachings, which should inspire us to perform good works and acts of charity. It is not a reward, but a means to receive God's grace. Preparation through confession and repentance is crucial before partaking. Holy Communion symbolizes the union between the believer and Christ, affirming our commitment to His teachings.

The main reason why we should approach Holy Communion with spiritual diligence is not because the Son of God, His holy body, or His precious blood can be defiled by anything else, but rather because we are united with His flesh and blood. We must always strive to live in a manner that avoids the obstacles that Satan, who is jealous of our salvation, places in our way to tempt us and lead us into sin. In order to save ourselves from sin, we must participate in the holy ceremony of receiving the flesh and blood of Christ, which we take for our eternal salvation. We must spend our lives in faith and conduct, doing righteous works. Christian vigilance is necessary because Satan often throws subtle obstacles in our way.

If we stumble and fall into sin after receiving Holy Communion, we must repent and confess our sins to the priest. We should stop receiving Holy Communion for the time being, complete our penance, and seek advice and guidance from the priest before resuming Holy Communion. Once we begin to receive Holy Communion, we should avoid sins and offenses that would prevent us from approaching it. If we commit a sin that should not be repeated after receiving Holy Communion, we have dishonored this great sacrament and must repent and work to strengthen our spiritual purpose.

We should not take repentance lightly or assume that we can continue to repeat the same offense. We must strive to control our thoughts and emotions, live steadfastly in morals and faith, and quickly repent if we fall into sin. We must constantly strive to strengthen our spiritual purpose in order not to be separated from the Holy Communion.

In addition, there are certain rituals and beliefs that may be common in some places but are not in accordance with the Church's canon and tradition. When we encounter doubt or confusion, we should seek guidance from the Church fathers, teachers, and scholars to clarify the true teachings of the Church. We should not be led astray by beliefs or practices that are outside of the Church's system. As St. Paul advised Timothy, "Avoid godless chatter, because those who indulge in it will become more and more ungodly" (2 Timothy 2:16).

text: Mr. Yohannes, what is the history behind St. Mary meaning what did she do in her life that pleased God? To add on to this why do we have so many icons in our church, ecspecially the Icon of our Lord Jesus Christ and St. Mary? Why is there the Trinity 3?

Beloved in Christ, peace be unto you. It gladdens my heart to address these soul-searching inquiries.

The Blessed Virgin Mary, ever revered as Theotokos (Mother of God), embodies humility and obedience which found favor with God. Her acquiescence to God's will—"Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word" (Luke 1:38)—exemplifies her deep faith and submission. Her life, from the Annunciation to her presence at the Crucifixion and beyond, marks her as a pivotal figure in our salvation history, continually interceding for us as a spiritual mother.

Concerning the icons, they are not mere decorations but windows to the divine, aiding our contemplation and veneration. Each icon is a sacred invitation to enter into a spiritual dialogue with the Holy. As a revered father proclaimed, "The beauty of the images moves me to contemplation, as a meadow delights the eyes and subtly infuses the soul with the glory of God." Hence, icons like those of Christ and St. Mary help focus our worship and reflect the incarnate reality of the Word made flesh.

The Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—represents the Christian doctrine of one God in three persons, a profound mystery of our faith that emphasizes the perfect unity and distinctiveness of each Person of the Godhead. This foundational belief shapes all aspects of Orthodox theology and worship.

Now, dear soul, may I ask you to reflect on how the humility of the Theotokos might inspire your own walk with Christ? How can the presence of sacred icons in your daily environment draw you closer to the divine mystery of love that surrounds us?
