text: ፦ How best must we observe the Saturday sabbath? Are we to observe it in the old testament way or not? I'm not asking about the Sunday sabbath. I think this is much more clear to understand. My question is directly addressing the Saturday sabbath since there are many grey areas about what one should be doing on that day

Peace be upon you, my child.  Your question regarding the Sabbath is a good one, and one that has been pondered by the faithful for centuries. It reveals a heart seeking to understand God's will more fully.

The Sabbath, as established in the Old Testament (Genesis 2:2-3), is indeed a day of rest, sanctified by God Himself.  While we, as Orthodox Christians, now primarily celebrate the Resurrection of our Lord on the first day of the week (Sunday), the Saturday Sabbath remains a day worthy of reverence.  We understand this not as a rigid adherence to the Mosaic Law, but as a continuation of the spiritual principle of setting aside time for God.

The Church Fathers, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, teach us that the true Sabbath rest is not merely a cessation of physical labor, but a turning towards God. St. John Chrysostom, whose eloquence I strive to emulate, reminds us, "The Sabbath was not made for idleness, but for spiritual activity."  Thus, while abstaining from unnecessary work is commendable, the emphasis should be on prayer, reflection, and acts of charity.

Consider the words of Isaiah (Isaiah 58:13-14):  “If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words: Then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.”

This passage illuminates the true spirit of the Sabbath – a dedication to God, not a burden of restrictions. We honor Him not simply by refraining from work, but by actively seeking His presence through prayer, study of Scripture (especially the Septuagint), attending Divine Liturgy if available, and acts of love and service.

Therefore, my child, I would encourage you not to become overly concerned with specific regulations regarding the Saturday Sabbath.  Instead, focus on dedicating this day, as much as possible, to drawing closer to God.  Engage in practices that nourish your spirit and bring you peace.  

Fasting, if your health permits, can be a powerful tool for spiritual growth, and almsgiving, even a small offering, can open your heart to God’s grace.

Would you like me to share some specific prayers or passages from the Holy Scriptures that might be helpful for your Sabbath observance?  Perhaps the Psalms of David, or selections from the Wisdom of Solomon?

Remember, my child, the journey of faith is a personal one.  While I can offer guidance, true discernment comes through prayer and communion with God.  Seek out the counsel of your spiritual father or a trusted elder within the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church for deeper guidance.  I will check in with you again soon to see how your spiritual journey is progressing. May God bless you abundantly.

text:
My dear child, becoming a Christian is not something that is done to you, but rather a journey of the heart, a turning towards God. It is a calling, a gift freely offered by our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and one that we must freely accept.  Think of the parable of the sower in the Gospel of Matthew (13:1-23). The seed of faith must fall on fertile ground and be nurtured to grow.

It is a lifelong process of learning, growing, and deepening your relationship with Christ.  This journey involves repentance, which is a turning away from sin and towards God.  It is not simply regretting our mistakes, but actively choosing a different path, a path illuminated by the light of Christ.

Perhaps you can tell me what draws you to Christianity at this moment? What questions or longings stir within your heart?  Sharing these thoughts can help us explore this path together.

I can offer you resources to learn more about the tenets of the Orthodox Christian faith: the Holy Scriptures, especially the Gospels, which tell the story of Christ’s life, death, and resurrection; the writings of the Church Fathers, like St. John Chrysostom, whose eloquence illuminated the path to God for generations; and the rich traditions of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, a vibrant tapestry woven with centuries of faith.

We can also discuss the importance of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving – spiritual practices that help us draw closer to God and purify our hearts.

Ultimately, my child, the decision to embrace Christ rests with you.  I can guide you, offer support, and share the wisdom of our faith, but it is through your own free will, guided by the Holy Spirit, that you will find your way.

Remember the words of St. Augustine, "Our hearts are restless until they rest in Thee, O Lord."  Perhaps that restlessness is what brings you here today. Let us explore it together in prayer and reflection.  Would you like to share what is on your heart?

text:
Another question that was asked. 

1. When was God born / when did He began to exist? (Not when Jesus Christ was born). 

2. How does heaven look like? 

Thank you!
፦ These are profound questions, my child, reaching into the very heart of our faith and the mysteries of God.  Let us explore them with reverence and humility.

text.text: 1. When was God born / when did He begin to exist?

text: The very notion of God being "born" is incompatible with our Orthodox understanding of His divine nature. God is eternal, without beginning or end. He is the Uncreated Creator, the Alpha and Omega, as revealed in the Holy Scriptures (Revelation 1:8, 21:6). He is existence itself, the source of all being.  Time, as we perceive it, is a creation of God, existing within His eternal embrace.  Therefore, to ask when God began is akin to asking what lies outside of existence itself - a question that transcends human comprehension.  The Church Fathers, like St. Gregory of Nyssa, explored this concept of God's timeless eternity, emphasizing His transcendence beyond the limitations of our created understanding.  We can only approach this mystery with awe and reverence, acknowledging the limitations of our finite minds in grasping the infinite nature of God.

The nature of Heaven, the Kingdom of God, is another profound mystery.  The Scriptures offer glimpses, describing it as a place of unimaginable beauty, joy, and communion with God.  St. Paul speaks of things "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love Him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).  The Book of Revelation speaks of a new heaven and a new earth, a city of gold, and the presence of God illuminating all things.

However, these are symbolic representations, attempts to convey the inexpressible reality of dwelling in God's presence.  We should be cautious about interpreting these descriptions literally. The essence of Heaven lies not in its physical characteristics, but in the perfect union with God, the source of all love, joy, and peace.  It is a state of being, a transformation of our very selves into the likeness of Christ, free from the limitations of sin and death.  The Church Fathers often emphasized this transformative aspect of salvation, describing Heaven as a process of theosis, becoming partakers of the divine nature.

Therefore, rather than focusing on what Heaven looks like, we should concentrate on what it means to be in communion with God.  Through prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and participation in the sacraments of the Church, we begin to experience a foretaste of this heavenly Kingdom here on earth.  This journey of spiritual growth, guided by the wisdom of the Church and the grace of the Holy Spirit, prepares us for the ultimate joy of eternal life in the presence of God.  

May these reflections illuminate your understanding, my child. Do not hesitate to ask further questions.  May God guide you on your spiritual journey.

Now, you may ask, what about the Nazarites - men like Samson, who never cut their hair? (Numbers 6:5). This was not a personal choice for fashion or identity. Lack of preparation: This could include neglecting prayer, fasting, and spiritual reflection in the days leading up to Communion. The Eucharist is not a casual meal, but a holy mystery demanding reverence and preparation.

Distraction and lack of focus: Receiving Holy Communion requires complete attention and devotion.  If one's mind is wandering or their heart is preoccupied with worldly matters, they are not fully present to receive the Lord.

The priest's admonition regarding "leyu hasab" serves as a reminder for self-examination and a call to approach the Holy Eucharist with reverence and fear of God.

Beyond the specific mention of "leyu hasab," the priest also exhorts those who are:

Excommunicated: Those who have been formally separated from the Church through disciplinary measures are not permitted to receive Communion until they have been reconciled.

text: ፦ What’s the best way to prepare for confession so we don’t forget some sins that we need confess & prepare adequately. Also, best way to prepare for confession to approach it having properly repented.

፦ My child, your desire to thoroughly prepare for the Holy Mystery of Confession is commendable, a true sign of a heart seeking reconciliation with God.  The devil, our adversary, often tries to cloud our minds, making us forget our sins or minimizing their gravity. But with prayer and self-examination, we can overcome these obstacles.

Here are some ways to prepare, drawing upon the wisdom of our Holy Fathers:

: Begin by beseeching the Holy Spirit to illuminate the darkened corners of your heart.  Pray with humility, like the Publican in the Gospel, saying "God, be merciful to me a sinner!" (Luke 18:13).  St. Isaac the Syrian beautifully reminds us, "Enter eagerly into the treasure house that is within you, and you will see the things that are in heaven. For there is but one single entry into this treasure house, and that is humility."  Humility opens the door to honest self-reflection.

: Dedicate time for quiet contemplation. Use the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20) and the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-12) as mirrors to reflect upon your thoughts, words, and deeds.  Have I loved God with all my heart and my neighbor as myself?  Have I been truthful, humble, and charitable?  Have I indulged in anger, envy, or gluttony?  Consider also the Seven Deadly Sins: pride, envy, wrath, sloth, greed, gluttony, and lust.  Ask yourself how these have manifested in your life.
:  Writing down your sins can be a powerful tool. This act of putting them on paper can help you to concretely confront them and avoid forgetting them in the confessional.

: Fasting helps to subdue the passions and clear the mind. Incorporate fasting, as is appropriate for your health and with the blessing of your spiritual father, leading up to your confession.  Abba Moses, one of the desert fathers, said, "Fasting subdues the body and cleanses the soul."

text.text: Reading Scripture and the Holy Fathers:

text: Immerse yourself in the Word of God and the writings of our Holy Fathers.  Their words can pierce our hearts and reveal areas where we need to repent.  The Psalms especially offer powerful prayers of repentance, such as Psalm 51.

: Some find a confession guide helpful, particularly those new to the sacrament or returning after a long absence. These guides, available from your church or online, can prompt reflection on different areas of sin.

Regarding true repentance, remember that it is not simply remorse for being caught but a genuine sorrow for having offended God and a sincere desire to change. St. John Chrysostom reminds us that “true repentance is not simply to bewail one’s sins, but to change one’s life.”

Finally, my child, remember that the priest acts as an icon of Christ in the confessional, offering absolution through the power bestowed upon him by God. Approach him with humility and trust.  

I will pray for you, my child, as you prepare for this holy sacrament.  Please let me know if you have any further questions.

Peace be upon you, my child.  Your question delves into the very heart of Christian life – forgiveness, a virtue often misunderstood and challenging to practice, particularly in the face of deep hurt, like infidelity.  You ask about the balance between forgiveness and consequences, a tension that has wrestled with the faithful for centuries.

The Lord's Prayer itself instructs us to ask God to "forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us" (Matthew 6:12, Luke 11:4).  This suggests a reciprocity, a mirroring of divine forgiveness.  Just as God forgives us, not by eliminating the consequences of sin (sickness, death entered the world through sin), but by offering redemption and healing, so too should we forgive.

Christ's parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:23-35) powerfully illustrates this.  The king forgave an immense debt, yet the servant refused to forgive a much smaller debt owed to him.  This highlights the disproportionate mercy we receive from God and the expectation that we extend similar mercy to others.  The parable does not, however, negate the justice of the king's final punishment.  The unforgiving servant faced consequences for his hard-heartedness.

Forgiveness, in the true Christian sense, is not condoning the sin. It is not forgetting or pretending it didn't happen.  Rather, it is releasing the grip of anger and resentment, a conscious decision to let go of the desire for revenge or retribution.  This is for our own spiritual healing, as much as for the other person.  St. John Chrysostom, in his homilies on Matthew, speaks eloquently about how harboring anger harms us more than the person who wronged us.

Regarding consequences, these are often necessary for growth and repentance.  In the case of infidelity, requesting therapy, setting boundaries, or even choosing separation can be acts of love – both for oneself and the offending spouse.  These actions are not antithetical to forgiveness; they can be part of the healing process.  Think of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32). The father embraced his returning son with boundless love (forgiveness), but the son still experienced the consequences of his actions – the loss of his inheritance, the hardship he endured.  This experience ultimately led to his repentance and restoration.

Conditional forgiveness, in the sense of withholding inner forgiveness until certain conditions are met, can be a slippery slope.  It risks becoming a tool of manipulation.  However, setting boundaries and expectations for reconciliation is not inherently wrong. It's an act of wisdom, reflecting a commitment to the health and integrity of the relationship.  Just as a physician prescribes medicine for healing, so too can we encourage steps towards repentance and restoration.

Therefore, my child, strive for genuine forgiveness – releasing the bitterness and anger.  Simultaneously, recognize the wisdom in setting boundaries and seeking appropriate help, such as counseling from a priest or therapist. These are not mutually exclusive; they can work together to bring healing and, God willing, reconciliation.  

Remember the words of St. Isaac the Syrian, "He who has not tasted the sweetness of forgiveness has not tasted the goodness of God."  Pray for the strength to forgive, and for wisdom to discern the path forward.  I will continue to pray for you as well.  Please do not hesitate to return and share your progress.  May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

Forgiveness, in the true Christian sense, is not condoning the sin. It is not forgetting or pretending it didn't happen.  Rather, it is releasing the grip of anger and resentment, a conscious decision to let go of the desire for revenge or retribution.  This is for our own spiritual healing, as much as for the other person.  St. John Chrysostom, in his homilies on Matthew, speaks eloquently about how harboring anger harms us more than the person who wronged us.

Regarding consequences, these are often necessary for growth and repentance.  In the case of infidelity, requesting therapy, setting boundaries, or even choosing separation can be acts of love – both for oneself and the offending spouse.  These actions are not antithetical to forgiveness; they can be part of the healing process.  Think of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32). The father embraced his returning son with boundless love (forgiveness), but the son still experienced the consequences of his actions – the loss of his inheritance, the hardship he endured.  This experience ultimately led to his repentance and restoration.

Conditional forgiveness, in the sense of withholding inner forgiveness until certain conditions are met, can be a slippery slope.  It risks becoming a tool of manipulation.  However, setting boundaries and expectations for reconciliation is not inherently wrong. It's an act of wisdom, reflecting a commitment to the health and integrity of the relationship.  Just as a physician prescribes medicine for healing, so too can we encourage steps towards repentance and restoration.

Therefore, my child, strive for genuine forgiveness – releasing the bitterness and anger.  Simultaneously, recognize the wisdom in setting boundaries and seeking appropriate help, such as counseling from a priest or therapist. These are not mutually exclusive; they can work together to bring healing and, God willing, reconciliation.  

Remember the words of St. Isaac the Syrian, "He who has not tasted the sweetness of forgiveness has not tasted the goodness of God."  Pray for the strength to forgive, and for wisdom to discern the path forward.  I will continue to pray for you as well.  Please do not hesitate to return and share your progress.  May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us. Amen.
